THE SONG OF THE nerSE BROOM. I sing the crisp song of the house broom, So brisk and of nothing afraid, 'Me emblem of order and neatness, In the strong grip of mistress or maid. , For whether to whisk, sweep, or freshen, I sing and rejoice while at work, And my honest home thrust is at rubbish and&ust Wheresoever they rally or lurk. In drawing-room, boudoir, and chamber, I'm at home as in kitchen and hall, 'Upon doorsill, piazza, and stairway, "Swish I swish !" sounds my challenging tall.. .. I'm the tyrant Sloth's Nemesis; swiftly The chains of neglect I unloose. Room, room for the broom, .inactivity's doom, ; Sworn foe to defect and disuse! Over Axminster wool-and rag carpet • My march I impartially take, 'While my sister, theplumed feather duster, Head erect, follows fast in my wake. :Not a corner so dark but I search it, ' Not a crannY too deep to explore; -After which,-shoulder arms till the next daf .5 alarms Call me forth, thorsugh-paced as before. ' My queen, lovely woman, impels-me; ' . I'm her slave or defender at need, ;As many a foe will bear witness Whom a broomstick hath put to his specd. In her grasp, be it dimpled or bony, I'm the sceptre or drudge of her will, And my besotn-like course gathers deftirrs or force As her housewifely wishes I fill. :rmrthe sprite of an -arrangement, am the vassal of thrift; To woman, for man's better comfort, I am civilisation's best gift, ' While cleanliness—so runs the proverb— Is to godliness nearest allied; r Room, room for the broom, and sunshine and gloom, The housekeeper's glory and pride! --Leeds Weekly' 'Supplement. Nxiestai D. URNER,

THE LITTLE PHOTLE.,-,-M-Elly parents who are polite and-polished iletheir mannere towards the world at large are perfect boors inside the iiorne curie. What wonder if children areithe: same? /f a maelailould accidentally,' brush against *mother in the-street, Air-apology would be sure to follow; but who ever thinkacf offering an apo- logy to the little people whose rights are constantly being violated by their caeeless elders? Ter QUEEN'S FIRST COUNCII,—The demeanour of the Queen-on this difficult and agitztin,g occazion is described AS composed and clignilzal. She received the homage of the nobility without any-undue .excitement, and her de- livery of the address was an adzr.irable specimen of the clear and impressive -reading to,-which her Majesty has since accustomed the public. Occasionally she glanced • towards-Lord Melbourne for guidance; but this occurred • very seldom, and fat- the most part her eelf-possession was extraordinary. The quietude of manner was now and then broken by -touches of -natural 'feeling which moved the hearts of all preeent. Her Maiwty was par- • ticularly :considerate to the Royal Dukes, her uncles; . and whenthe Duke'offlussex (who was infirm) presented -' himself to 'take the ceeh ef allegiance, and was aboutto kneel, she ,anticipated his action, kissed his cheek, and said, with great tenderness of tone. and gesture, "Do not ; kneel, my uncle, for I am still Victoria, your ciece." On - the whole, that day was the most, memorable in tile Queen's life, and its-effects were.seen next morning man aspect ..of pallor and fatigue. Au inexperienced girl, only just eighteen, hti.tiven invested with a power which carried: with it the gravest responsibilities towards innumerable millions; and she had for the' first time to discharge the duties of the State—duties.of which she could heve had no practical knowledge until -then—under the affliction -of a personal lass, for therecan be no doubt that stile was attached to her uncle, the late King. The lonelyheight of regal splendour was never mote sharply or intensely • felt than by that young Princess in the first hours of her grandeur and -her burden: It 13 true that the death of Bing William was not unexpected, and that his niece had for-some years been familiarised with the fact that, in the ordinary ecurse of nature, she would one day ,succeed to the crown. But death is always SUrpriSing when it comes, and the new monarch had. seen little of ,the ceremonial life of courts before her elevation to the throne.--li'art .1".. of" Life and Tiaaes of .Queen meto,ria.„ WHAT IS AN ENGLISH' GENTLMIANI—A distinguished German juriatewriting in March, 1883,-to a friend of his and mine in -iEngland, added the follovAng Postscript:— Do you know any good treatise -on the duties and •character of a gentleman? It is a peculiarly English social type. Latould like to draw sp.a comparison with our Continental rules of reepectability."- To- this in- quiry only one,reply seemed to be possible, namely, that -no suchformal treatise has ever attained anf,reputation, if, indeed, it has ever been written; and yet.the thought -suggested itself—ls not the type one which, even in the estimation of its enemies and detractors, has certain •,characteristics of value, worth preserving, therefore, in a special monograph for the information of a curious posterity, to whom the type itself may be no longer accessible? Failing _such a. eionograph, it maybe worth -while to indicate, a few of these characteristics, which, 'though familiar in the present day, may yet form valu- able material for some future historian of the race. Ido not intend to draw such a comparison as the letter sug- gested between the gentleman of England and his CO- relative in Germany or France; that must be left to those more familiar with these Lsetei types. But it has been my lotto have much intercoerse, on tolerably equal terms, with a good many Eoglishman of all classes; and I have thus, perhaps, had a better chance than many men of studying and fixing that something the posses- sion of which makes a man emphatically a gentleman,— a something which most Englishmen are quick enough to detect, but which they do nett find it by any means easy to define. If I could but transfer to these pages a real portrait—such a portrait as Velasquez or Vandyke would nave painted—of one of Vile many true gentle- men I have known, the work would be three-parts done to my hand. But such portraits are not new painted, or can we hope much from the more elaborate and fuller likeness which may be drawn in a good biography. Such men do not get their biographies written--it is not the custom of their class; or, if they do, it is not the qualitiee -which -marked them as gentlemen that are likely to be brought into prominence. This, then, is my definition e Agentieman is one to whom discourtelay is a sin and farsehood a crime.--Satimed Resiee. ForiintheAden days, not only was the Christmas holly and 'mistletoe displayed in hall and kitchen, but every season gave its proper flowers or shrubs to adorn the , English. home. - - Bunn 1)1nm-en. —,Charles Whymper, the veteran traveller, .bas. said—" (ke of the beauties of an English sumneerlandsoape is the glorious blue you get over dis- tant billsnnd country side. The captious may grunible that we getso few sunny days, but even they will have to allow that when it.does shine the sun here shines on the loveliest landscape ccuntry almost in the world. The hmount of -damp there lain, our land causes atmespheric .effects which areancomparably finer than those obtained in a dry climate. Distance takes its right place, :and • 20 miles away do not, as in Egypt, or even Italy, 14 Deem to be se close toyou as objects 20 yards off. One. cften wonders what•is the principle which gieres the air ge.n azure .cOlour.,and,why it is so much more marked at .some periods than at °them. There are days when,orily iii:stant objects take thia blue, and there are others when it seems to pervade things nearer at hand: sometimes it only touches the ;hills on the horizon, and then again At ,ecmes closerand gets under the shadows of hedges and 'into the recesses of woods and copses:" 'On a recent voyage of the City of Rome, Mr. P. E. Barnum was a ,passenger. At a concert 'given on the ship he was the preskling-genius. Heepened the even- ing with numerous anecdotes of his earlier days. Among' others, he told how he once bought a magnificent coach- dog, for which he paid fifty dollars. He said he was beactifully marked, but unfortunately he was caught in a heavy shower on the clay after he bought him, when, presi)! he was changed: into an ordinary cur, the spots having been ingeniously painted upon him. He went to the 4znan from whom he had purchased him_ He acknowledged the sale,hut said his clerk had forgotten to send the umbrella whieh,always wentwnth the dog, as be4could not stand the rain. Mr. Barnum closed the entertainment by giving specimens of legerdemain. His greatest trick, he said, had never been equalled in this , country or any other. He ,brolie a biscuit into three piec,es,esked some one lathe. audience to mark them, so that they could be readily identified. Then he asked for ; 'three hats, and placed a piece under each hat. Then ,once mere asking the :gentlemen if they were sure they would recognise the pieces again, he deliberately ate each piece. "-Now, ladies acid gentlemen, the most wonder- ful part of the feat appears. I will place all three of these plows of biscuit under one hat,ie you will choose which hata shall be." Thelat was immediately chosen, when Mr. liarnum instantly placed it on his head. "The three pieces of biscuit are all under the hat," said ho; andas no one could gaineay it, he. closed amid shcuts of laughter.

A FREYCTI MuurnF.rt TRiat, —A trial of a man for murder- inz a traveller in a railway train has juct been concluded at the Seine et Marne As.;zts at Melum. A coachman named Meunier left Paris for Troyes in October by the last night' trait, and was never after seen alive-. lEs body was found seven weeks afterwards in a pit not far from the railway, . with a handktrchief tied tightly round the neck sad the pockets rifh-d. It has been proved on the trial that a man named Riliodore Andre mnrdered the deceased, threw him oat of the carriage, jumped out after him, and wheeled his body in a harrow to the spot where it was found. One cur- ious point about the crime was the way in which it was dis- covered. Andre was in prison' for some other crime, and was under suspicion at being a railway thief, when two I gentlemen who had been robbed identified him as the rob- ber. This caused him to be suspected of the murder, and his mistress on being qttestioned identified the handkerchief that was tied round the murdered man's neck as Andle's Andre s mistress and his rioter were charged with being accessories and with participation in other thefts. Die man was found guilty with extenuating citcumstances, and sentenced to penal servitude for We ; the mistress was sen- tenced to three years' imprisonment; the third prisoner was acquitted.

THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.. THE ORIGIN OF 'IM "DOMESTIC 'DUCK. There is almost as greats variety in ducks as in the larger breeds of fowls, andit is very generally accepted that the whole of these lrarieties 'of ducks owe their origin to the common wild, or IVlallard, duck. Of course, there are those who, regarding only the great differences between the *varieties, cannot accept this theory, but all the evidetice seems to be;in favour of it. One of the chief varieties, the Rouen, is marked in.the same manner as the wild duckeand it has been no very uncommon thing, as we khall presently show, for young birds of the wild species to be taken and tamed. Some remarkable -instances of this will be given later on. Accepting therefore for the present that the wild duck is the progenitor of all the breeds of ducks which are known to us, it may be interesting to learn a little with respect to its habits. The wild duck is found in all parts of Europe ;and "North 'America, and also in some parts of Asia. /t is 'migratory in its habits, and usually large numbers -ilylogether, assuming in their flight a T-shaped squad. Vaterton, the naturalist, thus de- scribes *their Whits :—'44Maishy places, the margins, of lakes, pools, and rivers,, as *well as brooks, rills, and ' ditches, are its principkt Places of resort at ell seasons. It walks with 'ease, even runs with considerable speed, swims, and on occasion dives, although not in search of food. Seed Of grarainke and other plants, fleshy and 'fibrous roots, 'worms, •mollusca) insects, small reptiles, and •fishesotre the principal objects of its search. In shallow water it reaches the bottom with its bills, keep- ing the hind part .of the body erect by a continued motion athe feet. -On the wet* it sits rather lightly, with the tall considerably inclined upwards; when aearchingundee the surface it keeps the tail flat on the -water, and when puddlying at the bottom:with its hind Tart up, it direetethetall backward. The male emits a low and rather-soft cry; between a croak and murmur, ,and the female- a louder and clearer jabber. Both on beingilarmedeand especially in flying off, quack; but the quack of the female is much louder. When feeding 'they are silent; but when satiated they often amuse themseilves With- various labberings, swim about, sp- a:wort& each other; move their heads backward and for- wards," duck" in the water, throwing it all over their 'ba,eks, shoot along its surface, half flying, half running, and, in short, are quite playful when in good humour. , Gladstone was a true patriot, a man of the highest ability, i and he believed he was a God-fearing man, that he was in- fluenced by the highest principles, not only of patriotism but religious sentiment and feelings. (Applause.) Alderman E. Johnson seconded the resolution, and in re- ferring to its terms said be might say on the part of the Liberals of St. Helens, at least, that they would only use legitimate efforts for the purpose of returning Mr. Sinclair. (Hear, hear.) He observed that owing to reasons to which he did not wish to allude the Liberal party of St. Helens were not united at the last election, and he believed if the Liberals had been united on that occasion Colonel Gamble would been the representative of St. Helens in Parliament. (Applause.) It was that consideration which prevented him experiencing that full amount of pleasure that he should, and he believed if Colonel Gamble had been returned he would have presented himself on this occasion. Not having the opportunity of accepting Colonel Gamble as a candidate they had the very best man in Mr. Sinclair. They had heard his history as given by the chairman, and he thought that histoty spoke for itself of the energy and the perseve- rance of the person to whom he alluded. If he was returned as their member none of them would have reason to regret the vote they gave him, and he hoped every Liberal in St. Helens would unite for the purpose of securing a victory on this occasion, (Applause.) The object in sending a mem- ber te the Commons House of Parliament as a Liberal was for the purpose of supporting Mr. Gladstone. (Applause.) As Alderman ,Cook had said there might be some little dif- ferences existing in the minds of some Liberals upon one question, but he asked them to consider whether because simply upon one question they differed with Mr. Gladstone they were to throw him overboard, he who had done so much for England, and put in his place the Conservatives who had never done anything for the benefit and advantage of the country. (Applause.) He thought Alderman Cook was justified in asking them to sink those differences, and let them be united for the purpose of securing the return of their candidate. (Applause.) When he looked back at the past history of Mr. Gladstone he saw upon every important occasion when he had introduced measures that the same things were said then as were said now. With respect to the Disestablishtnent of the Irish Church, he heard a person say, directly after the meeting in the Volunteer Hall, where Mr. Gladstone started his campaign, that hanging was too good for him. Such was the feeling in this country at the time, but the result of the measure had been to bring peace and happiness where it did not exist before, and his firm opinion was that if the present measure Was passed it would bring further peace to Ireland, that prosperity would at- tend the efforts of its people, and not only would it do good for Ireland, but it would do good for England also. (Applause.) Mr. Gladstone's conduct through life had been to protect those who could not protect them- selves. It was to the poor and the middle classes that his legislation had been principally directed and for what rea- son ? The rich could take care of themselves—(hear, hear)—and in times past they had protected their own in- terests. He asked them to support these measures which would result in an advantage and benefit to those who were unable to protect themselves. (Applause.) Therefore they should support Mr. Sinclair upon this occasion, and they should not let .Sr. Helens be disgraced as it had been dis- graced. (Hear, bear.) A town full of manufactures was represented by a stranger, and here they had one presented to them who knew the interests and the manufactures of St. Helens, and it could be said of him as it was said of Colonel Gamble, that knowing what was its best interests he was the proper person to repreeent them. (Applause.) The resolution having been carried, • Mr. Sinclair, in returning thanks' said: I can only say I am very deeply indebted to you all for the very kind ac- ceptance of my name as your candidate, and I soall do all I can to help you, and I am sure I may rely upon you doing all you can to win the election. (Hear, bear.) I hope I shall be able to carry cut your wishes in Parliament. (Ap- plause.) Alderman E. Johnson then moved and Mr. Henry Martin seconded a vote of thanks to the chairman, which was warmly passed. . The Chairman responded, and assured them he had great pleasure in being present. He only hoped when they got to the end of the candidature they would be able to meet with as much pleasure and as much unanimity as they bad that evening. They had a lot of hard work to do, and he hoped they would accomplish it like men. (Cheers.) Mr. Martin then called for three cheers for the " Grand Old Man," which were lustily given, and the proceedings terminated. As Mr. Sinclair left the Town Hall !'hearty cheers were given for " Our future member," which he appropriately acknowledged. Mr. A. Sinclair, J.P., on rising to address the meeting, was received with loud cheers. He said he was exceedingly grateful for the kind manner in Which they had received the announcement of his name, but he was more especially grateful to Colonel Gamble for the overwhelmingly kind words with which he introduced him to their notice. It was something to recommend him to them when he should have been able to retain such friendship from a man like Colonel Gamble for a period of considerably over 40 years. He was very gratefol to Colonel Gamble for the kind words he had said, and for all that he had done with respect to this election, and also to Alderman Cook and Alderman Johnson for their expressions. Mr. Sinclair continued : There is one kindness that Colonel Gamble probably unin- tentionally added to the many preceding, when he stated that he would call upon me to address you, for whatever my talents as to business, and whatever my faculties for re- membering long strings of figures may be, the making of a speech is not my province. When I reflect that the people of the United Kingdom have to send 670 members to the Parliament about to be elected, and that a very long ses- sion lasts a thousand hours, because they only sit five days a week, and so many hours in the day, I observe that a thousand hours gives an hour and a half for each man, and some take more, and so if everyone was deter- mined to be an eloquent orator we should have more ob- struction complained of than we have had in the past. If there is one point in the programme of our great leader that I think more overwhelmingly necessary than another it is that the question of obstruction should be dealt with. I am glad that the change of position by our opponents has brought them to see that the complaints we had made in the last Parliament were well founded, and that even dur- ing their short tenure of office in this Parliament they took some steps, which have been followed by the Liberal Government, for the much more efficient discharge of the business of the House. All such efforts would get a most cheerful supporter in me, and certainly if I should be re- turned as your representative in Parliament I should not be one to unnecessarily prolong the debates by unnecessary talking. (Applause.) I don't know that there is any need to go through a long string of Liberal measures and pro- nounce an opinion upon them, as the very fact that you are here shows that you are (as I have been from my youth) convinced Liberals. The questions we were discussing last year so earnestly are for the present shelved, although they must come on as soon as the op- portunity presents. (Applause.) The question of obetruction I have just alluded to, but on that important question affecting the convenience of us all in the country, and that Colonel Gamble mentioned, the question of regis- tration—the Government has undertaken to deal with that, and I don't know anything that will make it possible to get at the real sense of the people of this country than to make registration easy, and not that tabominable trouble it is at the present, when anybody can object to a hundred noters, and can cause them all sorts of trouble, and to wait hour after hour at the registration court, for the purpose of sup- porting their votes, which will be lost if they go away. By this means many votes are lost. That was one of the first things in Mr. Gladstone's programme, and it has not been forgotten since. Everyone is agreed that the land laws must be greatly reformed. (Applause ) It only wants time to enable the Liberal Government, if we have the good for- tune to keep them in office, to deal efficiently with them. One branch of the suhject they have dealt with in the Crofters' Holdings Bil Teat bill is through Parliament and is now waiting to receive the Royal assent. (Cheers.) A more crying problem is the land question of the sister island, which will be settled by Mr. Gladstone's great measure when. it is carried, as it will be, as Mr. Morley said (pointing to the front Opposition bench) "if not by us by you." The Conservatives were quite willing when they got in office to make more rash movements in that direction than ever we should be willing to do, but in one way or other that question will be put out of the way, and then there will be time to deal with the land laws of England, and we have men in the House of Commons who are pre- pared to deal with them efficiently. (Cheers.) Then I come to the question of Local Government. One half of England has no sort of local government of its owh at all. The rural parts compose one half of our population, w and e why should they not have the same rights possess in our boroughs, and have the power to look after all expenditure and check it if they find it is getting too extravagant? That is a measure also that is near at hand. Then we had a good dell of discussion dur- ing the last campaign about the Emp oh Liability Act and the Coal Mines Act. Both of these bills are being dealt with by committees, and I hope that the outcome of the de- liberations on the Employers' Liability Act will be to declare that under whatever sort of insurance men be induced to enter nothing shall be done that shall prevent any man who has met with an accident g l etting at east what the law gives ' him in the absence of these insurance clubs. (Cheers.) I think it is a very great advantage in the meters and men subscribing to a common fund, so that in the great majority o'n which the Employers' Liability Act could not f cases in they would receive such a sum as would prevent them give any remedy fro m getting into penury, but one absolute condition it seems to me in any legislation upon that point is to insist that from this club or the master every man shall be entitled to the amount of redress that the Employers' Liability Act was meant to give (Cheers.) I am sure it can be worked financially, and I am sure it is the only way in which justice can be done. I hope the Miners' Act will be made free from the complaints that were made at the time of the last election. I remember that pleasing meeting in this hall some time ago with reference to the pit-brow women, and the curious attempt made by some to object to them making an honest living in a perfectly reasonable anti decent dress. It is quite certain from what passed and what was said by some gentlemen who took part not only in this town, but at other places, that no interference of that sort with the liberty of the women will be allowed to pass. Everyone ought to have the liberty of earning, a living honestly as best they can, and I don't think it ought to be a liberty for men and take it away from women. THE LIBERAL. CANDIDATE FOR ST. HELENS. ADOPTION OF MR. A. SINCLAIR, J.P. A hastily convened meeting of the 'Liberal Six Hundred of the Parliamentary Borough of St. Helens to consider the resolutions passed by the Liberal Council on Thursday evening week, recommending Mr. Arthur Sinclair,.JX., as the Liberal candidate at the ensuing General Election, was held in the Assembly-room of the Town Hall, on Friday evening. Considering that the circulars calling the meeting had only been issued on Friday morning there was a large. attendance. The proceedings throughout were of a most enthusiastic k character. The chair was oc- cupied by Colonel D. Gamble, J P., the candidate at the last election, and he was supported, in addition to Mr. Arthur Sinclair,'JP., by Aldermen E. Johnson. and T. Cook, Councillors J. Forster and J. C. Gamble, Messrs. H. Martin, W..Middlehurst, N. Lacey, B. A. Dromgoole, H. L. Riley (registration agent), Mr. John Cotton, /ice. The appearance of Colonel Gamble and Mr. Sinclair was the signal for loud applause. At the request of the Chairman, Mr. Riley read the notice convening the meeting. ' •The Chairman, nho was received with warm applause, said in asking them to consider the proposal that had been submitted by the Council, he could not do so without ex- pressing regret that he could not offer to be their candidate on the forthcoming occasion. It had ffeen thought that it would be better for. the Liberal interest, which was what be hoped all present -would consider paramount to everything else, that he should not b 3 a candidate this time. It was twelve months exactly within a week since he (Colonel Gamble) first met the, Liberal Two Hundred of the Liberal Association for the same purpose that Mr. Sinclair met them that evening, and he could not but remember the way in which be was received, and the way in which be was sup- ported all through the candidature of that five and a half months prior to the election with pleasure. In thanking the Liberal party for the kiodness with which they received him, and the consideration shown to him during the whole time he eves their candidate, he could only ask that the eatne consideration should be shown to Mr. Sinclair. (Ap- plause.) 'To those that differed on minor points from Mr. Sinclair, he asked them to extend the same consideration as many of his (Colonel Gamble's) friends and most ener- getic supporters did to him when he differed from them on the subject of disestablishment. (Applause.) He asked them to remember that the point upon which the dissolution would take place was an important point, presented in the way it was, but the greatest and most important matter they had to decide was that of sending to Parliament a representative of the great Liberal principles they had been fighting for. (Applause.) If there was anyone present who differed from Mr. Sinclair on the point that the dissolution was upon, he (Colonel Gamble) hoped he would remember that Mr. sinclair did not differ from Mr. Gladstone on that point—(applause)—and had agreed as far as he knew with Mr. Gladstone's career. (Applause.) He asked them to remember that their duty was to return a man who would support Mr. Gladstone in his general policy whatever it might be. (Applause.) Perhaps he ought to say a word about Mr. Sinclair. No one there knew him so well as he (Colonel Gamble) did. A great many knew him very well, and be never beard of anybody who knew him moderately well that did not think a great deal of him. (Applause.) They all new very well that Mr. Sinclair had been brought up to business. He began with business life in the office of 1 Bolton and Preston Railway Company at Bolton, of which railway his father was secretary. Mr. Sinclair came to St. Helens before be was twenty years of age as manager of the St. Helens Railway, which at that time was in each low water that £lOO shares were not worth £5. He left that railway in 1865, when it was sold to the London and North- Western Railway Company, and its shares were worth £lO3. (Applause.) After observing that since 1843 to the present time Mr. Sinclair had been his (Colonel Gamble's) most in- timate friend, Colonel Gamble briefly touched upon Mr. Sinclair's marriage to the daughter of Mr. Robinson, of the firm of Boornes and Robinson, and said that in 1874 he came into the business with which he was connected. With regard to his public career, he thought he need scarcely tell them that Mr. Sinclair was a Commissioner of St. Helens before its incorporation, from 1847 to 1855, and for five or six years of that time he was chairman, and had been at the head of almost all the steps in advance which St. Helens had made. Mr. Sinclair had been a reader and student of politics since he was twelve years of age, and had been asso- ciated with all the political movements that had taken place in Lancashire since he came to St. Helens. When Mr. Gladstone in 1868 contested South-West Lancashire, Mr. Sinclair was one of the most prominent members of his com- mittee, and he was with him during almost the whole of the campaign. (Aroilause.) In 1880 he was on the com- mittee for Messrs. Hathbone and Molyneux, and he was one of the meat prominent members of that committee, and he (Colonel Gamble) might also stets that it WAS to Mr. Sin- clair that Lord Derby fitst declared that it might be pub- licly stetea that he was sick of Tory tactics, and would after- wards be &mud on the Liberal platform. (Applause.) He (Colonel Gamble) did not regret giving up the idea of repre- senting St Helens when he could do it with the prospect of being succeeded by a candidate whom he knew to be so much superior to himself on all points that were expected from a member of the House of Commons. (Applause.) He had no acquaintance anywhere that he believed knew so much of the history of the House of Commons and all in connection with it as Mr. Sinclair did, during the last 50 or 100 years. (Applause.) He did not know any man in the House of Commons who could lay his hand at such short ' notice upon any return, any division, or any information whatever relating to the House of Commons, and he must say if they succeeded in returning Mr. Sinclair for St. Helens they would have a most efficient representative for for the town. (Applause.) The question for them to de- cide was whether they thought Mr. Sinclair was a fit and proper person for them to fight for on this occaSion. (Ap- plaese ) Alderman T. Cook then moved the following resolution : That this meeting of the St. Helens Liberal Association cordially endorses the candidature of Mr. Arthur Sinclair for the represeetetion of the borough in Parliament, heartily recommends Mr. Sinclair to the electors, and pledges its members to use every legitimate effort to secure his return." (Applause.) He said he had no doubt when they received the circular announcing the candidature of Mr. Sinclair they were very greatly surprised—no more surprised than were the members of the council when it was told to them, with some regret and pain, that Colonel Gamble was unable to consent to be pot in nomination as a candidate for St. Helens. The council were very greatly surprised, after Mr. Sinclair's name was mentioned, because some of them, at any rate, conceived that it wee not practicable that Mr. einclair could have offered himself as a candidate, and he wanted to say, in passing, that it was through—should he say generosity, nay, the magnanimity of Colonel Gam- ble, in making it possible—(applause)---that Mr. Sinclair was able to offer himself to the electors of St. Helens as their candidate. Colonel Gamble had always stood high in their estimation, but he stood very much higher in his (Alderman Cook's) estimation that night. (Applause.) That act of him was an act of self-sacrifice, a noble act, and the generous act to plaCe Mr. Sinclair in that position to enable him to offer his services to them. (Applause.) Something had been said with regard to the fitness of Mr. Sinclair for the position. He wished they could have heard the tribute which Colonel Gamble paid to Mr. Sinclair at the council meeting. It was a most touching tribute, one which moved the heart of every member present. Colonel Gain- hie said that if they returned Mr. Sinclair as their repre- sentative in Parliament be ventured to believe there were not more than a dozen men in the House of Commons of greater ability than Mr. Sinclair. (Applause.) Alderman Cook proceeded to pay testimony to Mr. Sinclair's know- ledge of Parliamentary history, and said he was a man of prodigious memory and marvellous ability for figures, and he was eminently qualified to tike his posiiion in the House of Commons as the representative of St. Helens. (Applause.) The question before the electors was this—Were they to support Mr. Gladstone in the measures which be was bring- ing before the country? (" Yes," and cheers.) Had Mr. Gladstone, the leader of the Liberal party, to be deserted in this hour? (" No " and cheers.) Had he not led them and the country, year by year, to measures of great and incalcu- lable benefit to the nation? (" He has," and applause.) Should they now, when he was assailed not only by foes but by some of his friends, desert him and allow him to go down in obecurity. (Cries of "No," and "Never.") The .cuestion of the government of Ireland was a very abstruse one, but was there another man in the kingdom who was so able to grapple with that questirn as Mr. Gladstone? ("No.") In his speeches in Mid-Lothian he said that a measure of self-government for Ireland, if it was properly cons'ituted, would tend to the closer union of the people and the closer union of the nations, and he had brought his enormous ability and experience upon the subject, and there was not another man in the kingdom so able to draft a measure which was likely to meet the occasion as Mr. Gladstone had done. (Applause.) If Mr. Gladstone was again returned to power he thought it would be quite pos- sible to draft a pill which would prevent the evils which were prognosticated. (Hear, hear.) The latter clause of the resolution he had moved was very important, because they were under some disadvantage in not having Colonel Gamble with the weight of his influence as their candi- date. Cclonel Gamble would have got in without the slightest doubt—(applanse)—and it was a disadvantage in not having him as their candidate. It was also a disad- vantage in not having Mr. Richard Pilkington as the chair- man to lead them on as he did at the last election. They would all remember the energy and enormous labour he underwent in order to secure the return of Colonel Gamble —(applause)—and they could not help expressing sym- pathy in the affliction under which he was suffering, and he was sure they all offered a sincere prayer that God might Keen restore him to health again. (Applause.) There were therefore two disadvantages under which they laboured in the present contest, and for that very cause they must buckle on the armour, and they must be determined that they would do more than they did before. (Hear, hear.) The battle would be fierce and the contest would be severe, but he was sure if all Liberals in the town would sink their little differences—and he was glad that Liberals had differ- ences, for he admired principles which allowed a man to think for himself—and go in for the great Liberal prin- ciples. He believed the measure for Ireland would be a blessing to the people and the country. For the life of him he could not see why Ireland should not make its own laws. (Hear, hear.) He knew some people looked at it from a religious point of view, but don't let themselves do so or they would be. bigots. He believed in the truth, and he believed that the principle of Home Rule was right and just, and what was right and just ought to be done; Mr. I

which I am standing before you to-night. It has been felt that it was utterly impossible to think of any town like St. Helens returning any man who is not a supporter of Mr. Gladstone. (Applause.) I have for many years been con- vinced that there was no possible solution of the Irish problem but the giving to them not what we think good for them, but what they were willing to accept. (Applause.) It is no use us saying to the Irish—you ought to be satite.: fled with that. They are a nation, and have just as much right to a will of their own as re have, and until they have got that there will "" no peace between us. People say if you give Ireland sepa- rate Home Rule you cannot refuse it to Scotland. Ile more would I refuse it from Scotland if they wanted it. But, be- cause one couple need a divorce, because they cannot live 1, happily together, there is no reason why people who live ' happily should ask for one because the others have got one: (Laughter.) England and Scotland live together in that way. They each get a reasonable amount of their own ereY' and Scotland gets much of her own way, and she is tho- roughly content, and therefore there is no chance of a see*lr rate legislature for Ireland being followed, I think, by desire for a separate Legislature for Scotland. If she watin it I hold that she should have a right to it, but I cannot understand how we Englishmen who have supported ever/ other dependent nation on the Continent,or anywhere else wbe have called out for separation from an over-riding tyrareoli should deny Ireland a blessing which we have helped everin other nation to get. (Cheers.) I believe all natio : oe if left to govern themselves, will govern themselves roe% ably well. lam an Englishman, and lam conceited eo°11;5 to think that we Englishmen know how to govern ourselle-t better than any other nation, but Ido not therefore iTto to call every other nation unfit to govern themselYea,alloe sav—if they are not Teutons or Teutonic, it is °lvo, thinking aoont their being able to govern therose—e, All I can say is, I hold the right of all nations to lodell'its dent rule, As soon as they can feel fit for it as to wen:eat I hope they will all get it, and first of all, I hope thati'ctee nation which has suffered so much from wrongs infl es. upon it by England, wrongs many of them of malice Pod pense, through an anxiety to take money from th€t' arid wrongs committed by blundering atternws to Befer—ietee do good by giving them what we thought in our irteli, 1, was the best for them without consulting them et hope the long sores of hundreds of years standing "'. lot England and lreland are at length to be healed, and tben we shall live harmoniously side by side. (Cheers.) Wder. that time has come about, when we have learned to lin tter stand each other, then a closer union may come abcuobed by than before, and not like that of 1800 which was OW heir bribes which were given to recreant Irishmen to sell t the country, but it will be brought about and upheld 11 tpe hearty good-will af two free peoples seeing that it best thing for them to unite together. (Loud cheers) oer The representatives of the press then retired. Four 9, tiens were afterwards put to Mr. Sinclair. The first Are you favourable to the Land Purchase Bill, and do I'7 think that the amount of the proposed purchase 10°,ebt ought to be reduced? Mr. Sinclair replied that he thoita they ought to act on the great principle that maim, 3.00 them in the abolition of the slave trade and the abolibl'ere of purchase in the army, and not to give grudgingly Ci ked a great reform was the object to be attained. He was 3,5 be if he was in favour of the Local Option Bill, to whieu.ee replied that he preferred to speak of that subject Lipon. rh principle of a pepular control of the liquor traffic, of woc.o he was in favour. Mr. Sinclair s tid that he thought t_.• voice of the people ought to be final, and that. beyond ao.we power of veto, as has had been suggested for the regulatiote of the two orders in the proposed Irish Chamber, he did nue; believe in the powers of an hereditary Chamber to obstrtw or delay legislation. an Mr. Sinclair then retired, and after Dr. McNicoll a others had spoken in favour of his candidature, the resoltii tion was carried with enthusiasm and without a single ha° being held up to the contrary. THE IRISH RIOTS.- RIOTERS SIOT

IN SLIGO. The funerals of those shot during the riots at 131fa5te took place on Saturday. An overwhelming force of arl33_, men at all threatened parts effectually prevented the break of any disturbances. Order was maintained while ,e processionists were passing through the streets. Lar4, crowds assembled round the open graves. The scenes W7.e. very affecting, women wailing and men sobbing. The 'l, turn to town was conducted in an unostentatious macle; the mourners travelling in smell knots, and avoiding as possible hostile districts. The whole of the cost of t.l funerals is being defrayed by public subscriptions, Yrbi'ee are pouring in most liberally; and not only are grave purchased for each family, but it is intended to distribtle: money among the friends of the deceased, who are all ill OP abject state of poverty. Tho Serious rioting occurred in Sligo on Saturday night. eze disturbance originated in the circumstance that in t'it morning it was discovered that a portion of the coping 3 the entrance to the residence of the Roman Catholic Bishad had been removed during the night. The coping-stone ha„, been removed from one of the piers, and an attempt ha', been made to pull down the piers. The coping-stone a` the gate of Alderman Tighe, a Roman Catholic, had ale been torn down. In the evening crowds assembled, and 1,1! a short time the streets were filled with an excited mcc; They first attacked the County Clubhouse, the windows 0' which they smashed. The -Sligo Clubhouse was next at" tacked, and the windows were broken. The mob, meeting with no opposition, proceeded to the residences of the Pre,s: byterian and Methodist ministers. Having smashed tu: windows of these houses, they b.took themselves to he Presbyterian and Methodist churches, and in a feel minutes they demolished all the windows in these edifice; No attempt was made to injure the Protestant EpiscoPa; churches. The crowd then resumed the wrecking (Li' houses in the town, and broke the windows of all the bees!' in which it was known protestants resided. Most of the larlsr ness houses in the town were closed soon after the rioting bet: gan, bat the extensive warehouse of Mr. M‘Donagb, whi,e" was still open, was attacked, and was completely wreckel Mr. Davys, Sessional Crown solicitor' who had been abse at Ballymote Sessions, returned to find a mob breaking fcte his house. He discharged his revolver, and the mob re' treated. They then went to the house of a Mr. M‘Loughreir and broke his windows and did their best to smash in the door. Mr. M'Loughrey fired into the crowd and wounded e boy named Burns in the head. The lad, who is in a dalr gerous condition, was removed to the Infirmary. Alfleoug.o' rey was arrested, but was afterwards d scharged on bail. About ten o clock on Sunday morning a crowd gather in Knox-street, and the Mayor and o her Roman Cathollc magistrates appealed to them strongly to meintain the, peace, and not to commit acts of savagery which woula bring the town into disgrace. The people appeared not to heed the advice, and the magistrates called in a large force of seldiers who were under canvas at Ross's Point, four or five miles distant. These came into the town. The Riot Act was read, the soldiers fixed bavone's, and were proceed' ing to charge the people, but this was unnecessary', the crowd, seeing fer the determined attitude of the authoritier dispersed. Sixteen arrests were made. The Roman Catholic clergy exerted themselves in inducing the crowde to disperse. Mr. Morley was engaged from an early hour on Saturdai morning with the principal officials at the Castle, Dublin, on the subject of the Belfast riots. Frequent telegrams Passed daring the course of the day between the Castle acu tlse resident magistrates and other responsible officials in the disturbed districts. Although the 'disturbances seern t°, have abated, to guard against their renewal geVer4' regiments left Amiens-street early in the morning for the north.

At the coroner's inquest at Belfast, on Wednesday, °ll the body of Hugh Henderson, who was shot last Weds day, a verdict of wiful murder was returned against one two Belfast police, who has numbers on their collars, and could not, therefore, have belonged to the count/ force.

TITE RESCUE OF BOYCOTTED CATTLE.—On Saturdal• at Kilduff, county Clare the nine men who are alleged W have formed a portion Of the party, consisting of some hall' dreds, who on the 4th ins'ant assembled at Kilduff and Car; rkd off from the police and bailiffs 75 head of cittle an" eleven horses which were seized by tbe bailiffs for arrears of rent on a boycotted farm at Bonnavitree, near Tulla, were brought up from Ennis gaol under a strong escort of police With loaded rifles. Bands marched in processional order. through the town, and tc,ok up a position in the road in front of the the courthouse. Inspector WhAlan, acting upon instrti tions from the Government, obtained an adjournment for another week. One of the bench magistrates, Mr. Crotty said that owing to the lawless state of that district he would be prepared to accept only substantial bail, which was /al' mediately forthcoming. On their release the defendants re' ceived a great ovation going through the town. div.p: 111XitEIGN NEWS.

THE SOUDAN.—HEAVY LOSSES FROM SICKNESS. CASED, MONDAY.—The health of the troops quartered at ' itaaouan and other stations Iva the Nile is very unsatisfac- tory. No less than 150 death's have occurred lately from Onteric fever and heat apople..xy. while 710 invalids are un- q9r orders to leave for Cairo on Thursday next. Tea soldiers died within the last 24 hours. GREECE.—A STORMY SCENE. ATHENS, SATrRDAY.—A stormy scene took place in the tionse of Representatives to-night. A violent discussion took place on the bills for the dimination of the ntimber of dePuties and for the extension of electoral districts. The djournment of the House was moved by the Opposition, out was rejected by a majority of eleven votes. Subse- quently the bills both passed the second reading. The triumph of the Ministerialists was greeted with mucia en- thusiasm. ATHExs,MONDAY.—An inquiry is proceeding here regard- ing the causes which led to the capture of so many prisoners oY the Turks, and suspicions have been excited relative to the conduct of some of the Greek officers who are at pre- sent under arrest. Some of the men have also been detained in the ranks pending the result of the inquiry, although Many of them belong to the classes of the reserve which have been disbanded. THE BULGARIAN ASSEMBLY.—SPEECH OF PRINCE ALEXANDER. SOFIA, MONDA.Y.—The Bulgarian National Assembly was opened to-day by Prince Alexander, who in his speech, said he was happy to welcome .the first Assembly at which representatives of the Bulgarian nation from both sides of the Balkans were present. He expressed his gratitude to- Wards the nation, who had risen as one man for the defence Of their country, andthad sacrificed everything to rave its honour and liberty and the integrity of its teriitory. In conclusion the Prince stated that certain bills and proposals With that object would be submitted by the Government, Who, he was confident, would obtain the enlightened co- operation of the Assembly. C HOLE it.A AT TRIESTE. TRtEsTs, MONDAY.—A workman has died from Asiatic cholera. A woman, presenting all the symptoms of the disease, has also died. Precautionary measures have been
-- EGYP r AND

taken. SUICIDE OF THE KING OF BAVARIA. MUNICH, MOND.LI.—King Louis of Bavaria, while taking a walk at a quarter to six yesterday evening in the park of the Berg Castle committed suicide by throwing himself into the lake of Castle, Dr. Gudden, his Majesty's pri- nts physician, who was in attendance upon the King in consequence of his insanity, immediately jumped into the water in order to rescue his Majesty, hut was himself drowned in the attempt. It would seem that a violent struggle took place. There are many footmarks in the soil at the bottom of the lake, and several bruises on Dr. Gud- den's face. There are also two large and two small scratches on the right oide of his nose and forhead, which Vase the theory ot a struggle beyond all doubt. The King, before throwing himbelf into the lake, lead divested himself ef the two coats he was wearing. In consequence of the death of King Louis, the generals cf the army met in Tuer- ken Kasedne at ten o'clock this morning, and took the oath of allegiance to Prince Otto, the late King's brother, who assumes the title of King Otto 1., and to Prince Luitpold as Regent. A similar ceremony was gone through by troops in all other barracks. MUNICH, TuEsua.Y.—A poet-mortena examination on the remains of the late King of Bavaria has disclosed an ab- normal construction of the skull and degenerative process in the brain. A funeral service was last night conducted over the remains of the late King at Berg Castle after which the body was temporarily placed in a plain coffin and conveyed in a hearse to the Residenz Schloss, at Munich. The Empress of Austria sent a magnificent wreath from Peldaffing. It is officially notified that the English Court will go into mourning for three weeks—fro_rn the 16th inst. to July 7th, for theists King of Bavaria. Munlor, WRDNiSDIT.—The public lying in state of the remains of the late King began at eight o'clock this morning, the Old Palace Chapel being fitted up for the perpose. The chapel is densely thronged by a contincous stream of inha- bitants of the city and visitors from the provinces, who are arriving in large numbers. CONFEDERATION IN SOUTH AFRICA. CArarOwN, MAY 26.—1 n the Cape Legielative Council, on the 20th inst., a discussion took place on a motion that the time had now arrived when the several states, colonies, and dependencies of South Africa should be united into one Dominion under the federal principle, and that for the pur- pose of attaining this object the views of the different We- temments interested should be ascertained without delay. The motion was withdrawn. Sir Arthur Havelock, the Governor of Natal, has concluded parleying with the Zulus and Boers, and his decision has been submitted to the Boer- . Zulu Republic. It is understood that the Zulus repudiate any agreement with the Boers. THE FRENCH PRINCES. Rola, WEDNesDAY..—Although the Vatican disapproYes the bill for the expulsion of the Princes from France, it has decided not to take any action in the matter. THE LABOUR DISTURBANCES IN BELGIUM. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WaDNEsDat. The Speaker took the chair at 12-20. ASSISTANT REVISING BARRISTERS —ln answer to a ques- tion put on behalf of Mr. Maurice Healy, Mr. MORLEY ex- pressed a hope that the bill enabling the Government Is appoint assistant revising barristers when necessary, would become law this session. THE STATE OF EGYrr.—On the report of supply, Sir G. CAMPBELL asked what was being done by the commissioners charged with the Egyptian negotiations. He thought it quite time that the House should be made aware of whether there was any prospect of an early report from Sir Henry Drummond Wolff.—Mr. BRYCE replied that the question of the organisation of the Egyptian army was making good pro- gress, but the further papers on the subject were not yet in readiness for presentation to the House. As to Assouan, the mortality had been considerably exaggerated, and with re- gard to the administration of justice, papers on the subject would shortly be laid on the table. MEASURES ADVANCED.—The report was then received, and the Appropriation Bill brought in and subsequently read a first time The report of ways and means was re- ceived. The Customs Bill passed through committee. The Patriotic Fund Bill was read a second time, as was also the Metropolitan Board of Works Money Bill. The order for the seconding reading of the Liquor Traffic Local Veto (Scotland) Hal was discharged. The Contagious Diseases (Animals) Bill was read a second time, and other bills were advanced a stage. On the order for the third reading of the Parliamentary Elections Returning Officers Act, 1875, Amendment Bill, Mr. RITCHIE moved the omission of the schedule providing the mode in which the expenses of the returning officers should be charged upon the rates. On a division the amendment was negatived by 97 against 65. The bill' was reatha third time. The Coal Mines Bill passed through a committee, and was read a third time. The Mat- red Women Maintenance in case of Desertion Bill passed through committee, and was read a third time. The Revis- ing Barristers (Ireland) Bill was read a second time. The House adjourned at 5 o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THURSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat shortly after four o'clock. MISCELLANEOUS.—The Labourers (Ireland) Acts Amend- ment Bill was read a third time and passed.—The Post- office Sites Bill passed through Committee.—The Patents Amendment Bill was read a third time and passed.—A number of bills were brought up from the House of Com- mons and read a first time.—The Duke of ARGYLL asked wlaen it was proposed to take the second reading of the Conveyancing (Scotland) Bill. He intimated that on the order for the second reading he should move that it be read a second time that day three months. TORY OBJECTION TO THE RETURNING OFFICERS' EX- PENSES BILL.—The Marquis of SALISBURY: I beg to give notice that on the order for the second reading of the Par- liamentary Elections (Returning Officers) Expenses Amend- ment Bill I shall move that it be read a second time that day three months. Their Lordships adjourned at ten minutes to five o'clock.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Tnynsne.Y. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. e SALFO.RD ConroranoN.—The Salfo id Corporation Bill was read a third time, the Queen's consent on behalf of the. Ouchy of Lancaster being signified. Several orders enabl- ing private bills not disposed of at the end of the session to be resumed next session were agreed to. THE NEW HEBRIDES.—MT. BRYCE, referring to the New Hebrides ques ion, said the Government bad received assur- ances from the French Government that the French ships and troops de-patched to the islands had only been sent there for the temporary protection of French subjects, and that there was no intention to annex the islands, or to de- part in any way from the understanding as to their inde- pendence which had been come to with her Majesty's Government. THE BELFAST RH-yrs.—Mr. J. Mont,Eet stated that the Government had decided to issue a Commission of Inquiry into the recent deplorable occurrences at Belfast. The Com- mission would • inquire into the origin and nature ef the riots, the proceedings taken by the magistrates and other local authorities for their prevention and suppression, and the action of the police during the riots. THE EDUCATION ESTIMATES.—On the motion for the ee'cond reading of the Appropriation Bill, Sir L. PeAmin made a statement on the education vote, which, he said, showed au increase of £123,092 on tho sum expended last year. There had been a large increase all over the king- dom in school accommodation,and the increase in the amount of the vote was gratifying, inasmuch as it was caused by an increase in the average attendance and an increased amount of efficiency shown at the School examinat!ons. The daily average attendance (62 per cent of the children who ought to be at school) and the general average regular attendance (76e4 per cent.) showed -an improvement over preceding years; but although they had done much a great deal more remained to be done. The Department was un- able to reeist the pressure in the direction of technical edu- cation, and it would soon become necessary for the House to give them advice upon it. The question could not be de- cideel on a largo scale until they had had an opportunity of finding the mind of Parliament on. the whole question of technical education.—Sir HENRY ROSCOE was glad to hear Sir L. Playfair speak out to decidedly on the important subject of technical education, which he believed the country now generally felt should be introduced into our elememary school sys- tem. In education there were many matters, especially manual instruction, that might with great advantage be taken up by the Science and Art Department.—Mr. MATHER made some remarks upon the sew era which the Vice-Presi- dent had opened out before the House.—Mr. STANLEY LEIGHTON dealt with the subject of over-pressure in Board echools.—After some further discussion, the Appropriation Bill was read a second time. MIcCELLANEOUS.—SeveraI measures were forwarded a stage, and the House went into Committee on the Tithe Rent Charge Redemption Bill, which passed through Ccm- mittee and was read a third time.—On the motion to go into Committee on the Shop Hours Regulation Bill, Mr. C. BENTINCK moved that the House should go into Committee on the bill thieday three months. Lie refused to discuss the merits of the bill, which were very small, at a period of the session when the House was in extremis.—Sir M. H. BEACH Said the bill was introduced with a most benevolent object, but the bill as it now stood would fail to accom- plish its object, because there was no one to enforce its provisions.—Mr. BROADHURST observed that from the chorus of opposition which had proceeded from the other side, one would imagine that Parliament 'was being asked for the first time to legislate in restraint of the hours of labour.—Mr. EMBER spoke in opposition to the bill.—The House then divided—For the amendment 23, against 61-38 —The House went into committee on the bill as amended, sitting till a late hour.

ROUNDEES. WIDNES AND DISTRICT V. UNION (LlN'Ertrom.)—This match cime off on Saturday, on the ground of the Widnes Club, the district team comprising members of the Widnes, Simms' Cross, Beaconsfield, St. Paul's, and White Star Rounders Club. The borne team batted first, but made no stand against the bowling of Coke (the Union captain), the innings closing for 12 runs. The visitors then went in against the bowling of Waldron (W.R.C.) and ran up a score of 49 runs, thins leaving the home team 37 runs be- hind. In the second innings the home team made a bad start, but owing to Waldron, Heves, and Bate, who made 32 runs between them, batting in very good style, the total at the closing of the second innings amouated to 41 runs. The Union's second attempt realized a total of 50 runs, the visi- tors thus winning the game by 46 runs. After the match the visitors were entertained to tea by the home team, which was provided by Mrs. Cookson, Stanley Hotel, Mill- field, who gave every satisfaction.
