The annual conference of the Lancashire and Cheshire Association of Baptist Churches was held at Chester, on Wednesday, the Rev. J. Pvwell (Stockport) presiding. The secretary's report showed that the °limber of churches was the same as last year, with an increase of membership in the various districts. DISUNION IN THE PRIMROSE LEAGI7E.—It would seem from the fetter of "An Executive Officer" that all is not peace and harmony in the ranks a the Primrose League. The organisation, we are told, now numbers 300,000 electors. but this formidable voting machine cannot tila made to run straight. At Hackney the Leaguers want a candidate of their owo, and will net support the Unionist Liberal who will oppose the Attorney-General. "In many other places," says the "Executive Officer," with then grief, "the Prim- rose League has not decided on its action some are in favour of total abstention at the comiog election, others will not work for any candidate who will not pledge himself to follow Lord Salisbury, &c." We may assume therefore, that a League which has spocially charged itself with the maintenance of the fabric of the British b mpire, now sup- posed to be tottering to its fall, is unable to maintain unity among its own members.

div.head: EXAMI
div.p: THE EXAMI
THE ELECTION CAMPAIGN. Mr. C.E. Sebwann ha consented to stand as the Liberal

candidate for Nortlt Manchester. Wish,Ju.—Mr. C. M. Percy, Gladatoniau Liberal, will op- pose the re-election of Mr. F. S. Powell, M.P. • Lord Randolph Churchill has consented to stand again for his present constituency, South Paddington. The Rochdale Liberal Council have adopted Mr. T. B Potter, M.P. as the Liberal candidate for the borough. Mr. Arnold Forster has consented to become a Union- ist Liberal candidate, to costest Mr. Fry's seat at Darling-
ton. Lord Edward Fitzmanrice, formerly Under Secretary for Foreign Affairs, will stand as a Liberal Unionist for East

Per $01;i ce. The Mayor of Waterford bas convened a sleeting of the Town Council to confer the freedom of the city on Mr. Gladstone. Mr. Mills Mattinson wagon Tuesday selected the Conser- vative candidate for Dumfries; Burghs. He opposes Mr. E.
Noel (L.U.) Mr. William Summers, former member for Stalybridge, has consented to oppose Mr. E. A. Leatham's re-election for

Huddersfield. NEWCASTLI-ON-TYNB.—Sir Matthew White Ridley ac- cepted the requisition on Wednesday night to 'stand as a Conservative candidate. Mr. Wm. Agnew, M.P., has accepted the invitation of the Liberal Council, and will again contest the Stretford Divi- sion at the coming election The Council of the Liberal and Radical Association of North• East Bethnal Green have selected Mr. George M.P., as the ministerial candidate. At Chester, on Wednesday night, Earl Spenzer addressed a great meeting of Liberals on the subject of Home Rule, ani strongly supported the policy of Mr. Gladstone. The " standard " says—We understand that the influence of Lord Derby in Lancashire will be given to those candi- dates—Liberal and Coneeryative--who are opposed to the
Home Rule Bill. Mr. Rathbone, Mr. Byran Roberts, and Mr. Jones Parry will be invited to stand for Carnarvonshlre again, the Liberal Association having approved of their votes on the

Home Rule Bill. The Liberal Council for the Spalding Division of Lincoln- shire on Tuesday selected Mr. Hailey Stewart, of St. L-onard's, as ministerial candidate, in opposition to Mr. Finch-Hatton (Conservative). Mr. Bright has consented to have his name submitted to the Liberal Council of the Central Division of Birmingham, feeling that he cannot withdraw from Parliament if the con- stituency place confidence in him. The Oldbam Liberal Six Hundred have approved of Mr. J. M. Cheetham, of the firm of Cheetham and Sons, cotton spinnets, Shaw, as a candidate, along with Mr. Hilbert, for the representation of the borough. Colonel Schwabbe, M.P. for the Middleton division, whcse vote against the Home Rule Bill excited great dis- satisfaction amongst his constituents, on Thursday night announced that he will not seek re-election. Sir Wilfrid Lawson has accepted the invitation of the Liberals of the Cockermouth division of Cumberland to be- come their candidate. He enthusiastically support Mr. Gladstone's policy of conciliation to Ireland. At a meeting of the Liberal Five Hundred for the Aber- eromby division af Liverpool on Thursday night, Sir T. Brassev, M.P., was unanimously adopted as the Liberal can- didate for the division at the approaching election. Mr. R. Leake, M.P., has been adopted as the Liberal candidate for the Radcliffe-cum-Farnworth Division of South-East Lancashire. Mr. Leake will be opposed by Sir Frederick Milner, late Conservative candidate for

York. A meeting of Lib-ral deieqates, held at Liskeard, on Tuesday, decided by 58 against eight votes not to support Mr. Courtney's candidature, and a committee was instructed to obtain another candidate to contest the division as a

• ministerial The annual meeting of the London and Counties Liberal Union was held in Londou on Wednesday. Mr. John Mor- ley, M.P., was re-elected chairman of the Union. A resolu- tion a;Troving Mr. Gladstone's Home Rule Bill was carried

by 75 to 10 votes. It is expected by the Conservative party that a large number of county constituencic.s held by Conservatives will not be contestod, and that by Wednesday, the 30th instant, several unopposed returns to the new Parliament will have

• • been announced. Sir Horace Davey, the Solicitor-General, has accepted the invitation of the Svockport Liberal 400 to contest the borough with Mr. Joseph Leigh, the ex-mayor, as a col- league. Both the gentlemen are pledged to support Mr. Gladstone's scheme. Mr. R. N. Philips, late member for Bury, has resigned the Presidency of tho Liberal Association of the Stratford-on- Avon Division of Warwickshire, and Lora Camperdown the Vice-presidency, because of Lord William Compton's vote in favour of the Irish Government Bill. The Liberal Four Hundred of North Lonsdale on Thurs- day decided by an overwhelming majority to bring forward a Gladstonian candidate against the sitting Conservative member, Mr. Ainslie. In consequence of this decisioa Lord E. Cavendish, M.P., who presided, left the meeting, accom- panied by a number of his friends. A manifesto, signed by Lord Derby and other Liberals, was issued on Tuesday to the electors of Liverpool and dis- trict. It states that a Liberal Unionist Association for Liverpool and neighbourhood has been formed, and it ap- peals to Liberals who place patriotism and duty before all other considerations for their support in returning Unionist

Liberals. Mr. Chamberlain presided at the inaugural meeting of the new Radical Union held in Birmingham on Thursday. In a speech which he delivered he protested against the attacks which had been made against the new organisation, and said it was one of their chief objects to maintain within the ranks of the Liberal party a full representacion of Union- ist views on the Irish question. Lord lddesleigh, speaking on Tuesday afternoon at a Conservative demonstration at Patshul Park, near Wolver- hampton, in reply to a *vote of confidence in the Conserva- tive leaders, said he believed the majority of the people of England were determined to maintain the Union between Great Britain and Ireland, not for the sake of Great Britain only, but for the sake of Ireland herself. The Duke of Westminster has thrown the weight of his influence into the Conservative scale at Chester. On Thurs- day night a "Unionist " meeting was held in that city, and Lords Henry and Arthur Grosvenor appeared on the plat- form. The Duke wrote, in a letter read by the chairman, that it was now the duty of all men, Liberal or Conserva- tive, to work for the maintenance of the Union. It was authoritatively announced, on Thursday, that Mr. John Slagg had accented an invitation from the Liberals to contest the Crewe division of Cheshire, Mr. Slagg, how- ever, although be had promised to place his services at the disposal of the party, on Thursday withdrew his consent. The reason for this alteration is said to be that Mr. Slagg intends to contest the Darwen division against Lord Cain- borne. The fortnightly meeting of the Irish National League was held at Dublin on Tuesday. Mr. John Dillon presided, and referred to Mr. Gladetone's manifesto as a most straight- forward and courageous declaration of pone:,. The recent riots at Belfast he attributed to the conduct of Lord Ran- dolph Churchill and Mr. Chamberlain in appealing to the , worst passions of Orangemen.—Mr. Healy suggested that juries should return a verdict of murder against Mr. Cham- berlain instead of against the police. ACCRINGTON DtvistoN.—Mr. Joseph Francis Leese, bar- sister of Working, was on Wednesday evening adopted by the Liberal Council for the Accrington division by a vote characterised by great warmth and unanimity.- Mr. Leese gave an exposition of his views, declaring himself a thorough supporter of Mr. Gladstone and his policy. Mr. Leese. who is well-known as a cricketer, contested Preston in 1888, was formerly a cotton spinner at Preston, and is a J.P. for Lancashire.

General sympathy will be felt for Mr. G. W. Latham, M.P., who won a seat in the Crewe division of Chester at the last General Election. The hon. member, who has been engaged for some years in unsuccessful attempts to break down Tory domination in Cheshire, was prostrated for many weeks by illness after his victory, and he now an- nounces that his ill-health compels him to give up all hope of remaining in Parliament. The Crewe Liberal Executive have passed a resolution expressing their sympathy and re- gret, and are now loeking.out for another candidate. Buns.—On Wednesday night a meeting of the Liberal Association was held to consider the position of Sir Henry James in relation to the Liberals of the borough. A mo- tion was made that be was a fit and proper person to repre- sent the borough. An ameedment was moved (after Sir Henry had delivered a long address) recording unabated confidence in Mr. Gladstone's Government, and approval of their endeavour to settle the Irish question, and further de- claring that no candidate will he acceptable to the electors who is sot prepared to adopt Home Rule upon the lines of Mr. Gladstone's recent address.—The motion was carried by 118 to 64. A largely-attended meeting of Liberals was held at Mid- dleton, near Manchester, on Monday night. The followinz telegram was read from Colonel Salis-Schwabe, the member for the division who voted against the Government on the Horns Rule Please inform meeting I accept Glad: stone's proposals that Ireland ehould, under well-considered conditions, transact her own affeirs. I voted against the bill because I held conditions Out well considered. Wish to address constituents as soon as possible." The telegram was received with groans and cheers. A resolution in favour of Mr. Gladstone's bill was carried by a large mejoritv, and the Liberal Council of the division was ia- structed to select a candidate holding similar views. BARROW.—Although the Council of the Barrow Liberal Association has repudiated Mr. Caine, that gentleman is be- ing brought out by those Liberals who differ from the action taken by the Liberal Four Hundred, and oommittee- rooms for Mr. Caine have already been engaged. Mr. Schneider. who was defeated by Mr. Duncan at the general election, has been asked to stand again for the Conserva- tives, but that body have not yet determined on what action they will take. Many are strongly in favour of the re-election of Mr. Caine. The Liberal Four Hundred have not yet secured a candidate. Mr. Caine, in his address to the electors dated Wednesday, sets forth at length his ob- jections to the Home Rule Bill. The Marqu's of Salisbury, speaking on Saturday after- ternoon at a demonstration of Hertfordehire Conservatives, held in the grounds of Hatfield Park, denounced the Government Home Rule Bill as containing proposals which not even the wildest revolutionary had up to that time con- ceived. The issue now th-fote the country was not merely the setting up of a legislature at Dublin, but it involved also the executiie Government of Ireland to mos who were
NE

In sentiment and wish separatists, and when once the separ- ation of Ireland from Great Britain WdS effected, Ireland might at any time become a hostile power at our very door. Finally, he protested against placing in the hands of the Nationalist party the fate of their friends in Ulxter and the power and integrity of the empire. Lerd John Manners and Sir R. E. Webster, M.P., also spoke. MR. RYLANDS AND HIS CONSTITUENTS. , Mr. Peter }Wends (accompanied by Mrs. Ryland') ar- rived at Burnley on Tuesday afternoon, and, by appoint- ment, met a section of the Executive at his hotel quarters, The Thorn. He had expressed his desire to meet the whole of the Executive, but the Gladstonian portion of the mem- bers, who are seeking a new candidate, did not feel at liberty to parley any longer. A meeting of the Liberal 300 was held on Tuesday evening in the Mechanics' Institution, under the presidency of Alderman Baron.—A letter from Mr. Rylands was read by the Chairman, who sugeested that the subject of the evening should be approached with great calmness and forbearance. Two names would be placed before them for consideratioe.—Councillor Collinge then gave the names of Mr. Peter Rylands and Mr. Wm. Summers, late M.P. for Stalybridge.—Mr. Drew, of Lower- house, said: It gives me great pleasure to propose that Mr. Rylands is a fit and ttroper person to represent this borough in Parliament. Continuing, Mr. Drew eulogised Mr. Rylabds' past conduct, and thoroughly agreed with the I stand he had taken in regard to Mr. Gladstone's bill.—The motion was seconded by Captain Berry, and supported by a gentleman from the body of the hall.—Mr. David Holmes called attention to Mr. Drew's remarks, as well as those of the seconder, by which they took the opportunity of an- nouncing that if they were in a minority that evening they could not join the majority. He (Mr. Holmes) thought if this was the case, they might as well not prosecute any business, but all go home.—Mr. T. Taylor said that he in- tended to vote for Mr. Rylands, but if the majority were against him, he would go over to the majority, so that the vote might be unanimous. This sentiment was received with loud cheers.—The Rev. J. W. Clarke thought Mr. Peter Rylands, to be consistent, should follow the example of his new chief, Mr. Chamberlain, who had said that so far as ha was concerned, if he was not supported by the Liberal Association, he would not go into Parliament by Tory votes. The vote was then taken for and against Mr. Rylands. In a very quiet and orderly manner, the meeting separated themselves on both sides of the room, four tellers being ap- pointed. The numbers were announced as follows : For Mr. Rylands Against This master having been settled, Mr. Summers, the late member kr Stalybridge, was proposed as a fit and proper person to represent the borough in Parliament, the veting being as follows : Mr. Summers 207 Against On the substantive motion being put about 10 or 12 of Mr. Rylands' supporters left the room, "one by one," and only about four hands were held up against Mr. Summers, the substantive motion being taken by a show of hands.—A vete of thanks to the chairman concluded the meeting. Mr. William Summers has declined the invitation of the Burnley Liberal Association to contest the representation of the borough, Mr. P. Rylands has definitely intimated his intention to take the opinion of the electors on his conduct. The Three Hundred will be again called together at an early date. On Wednesday evening Mr. Rylands issued an address to the electors of Burnley, in which he says:—"l have decided upon asking your support as a Liberal Unionist. I shall stand upon the platform qf the maintenance of the legisla- tive Union between Great Britain and Ireland. I have al- ways been and still am in favour of justice to Ireland,' but in my opinion the Government of Ireland Bill introduced by Mr. Gladstone and rejected by the House of Commons was not a measure of justice.' Mr. Rylands, M.P., on Thursday night addressed a large meeting in the Burnley Mechanics' Institute, and spoke, amid considerable interruption, in !ratification of his action lin regard to the Home Rule scheme. A resolution approv- ing Mr. Itvlands's candidature was adopted by a large ma- jority. The Liberal Executive have selected Mr. Alderman Greenwood, a prominent resident of Burnley to oppose Mr. Rylands as a Gladetonian Liberal.

LORD HARTINGTON AND HIS CONSTITUENTS. At Saturday's meeting of the Rossendale Liberal Three Hundred it was seated that Mr. Gladstone had expressed a desire that Lord Hartington should not, be opposed in Ras- sendale. Mr. Barlow, of Haslingden, wrote to Mr. Arnold Morley asking if this were true, and he has received the following telegram in reply :—" Treasury Terrace, West Strand.—Mr. Barlow, Haslingden,—The Prime Minister has not interfered, and does not wish to interfere with the decision of the Liberal party in Rossendale." The executive of the Conservative party have decided to recommend the council& which meet next week to offer no opposition to Lord Hartington's return. The Liberal Executsve for the Rossendale Division met to consider what steps should be taaen in view of the resolution adverse to Lord Hartington's candidature passed by the Liberal Council on Saturday. The position of the party was fully discussed, and it was decided to adjourn the consideration of the question of a new candidate until Lord Hartington's manifesto has been issued. The telegram from the Government Whip announ- cing that Mr. Gladstone th3es not desire to interfere with the Rossendale Liberals has given great satisfaction among the Radicals of Rossaidale. A number of the Nonconfor- mist ministers in Rossendale have subscribed their names to the following :—" That we, the undersigned Nonconfor- mist ministers, are of opinion that on the dissolution of the present Parliaenent a candidate should be elected to contest kossendale at the next election who is 'in favour of the I principles advocated by the Government for granting auto- nomy to Ireland, and who is also in favour of religious equa- lity, including diseetablishment."
THE MANIFESTO.

Lord Hartington's Manifesto, in the shape of an address to the electors of Rossendale, was issued On Wednesday evening. His Lordship expresses his regret that his action on the Irish question has deprived him of the confidi nce of the majority of the representative Council of the Liberal electors of the division, but says the circumstances are so unprecedented and grave that he cannot accept as final toe decision of any body of his constituents. Tne premature dissolution has been brought about solely by the failure of the Government to secure the assent of the House of Com- mons to an Irish policy which had never previously been explained or even indicated to the country. He maintains that neither Parliament nor the constituencies ought to be invited to accept the principle of so vast a change until they have before them a plan satisfying conditions which Mr. Gladstone has himself declared to be indispensable. In hie opinion the question is one not so much of justice or of right as of expediency. The noble Marquis wither says that he has been compelled to conclude that within the lines of the plan of the Government it is impossible to devise any adequate protection for those who are admitted to need . it. That plan surrenders powers which the Imperial Government and the Imperial Parliament must retain if the first duties of government are to be dis- charged. While not prepared to commit himself to the details of any of the alternative plans which have been pro- posed, his Lordship says that Parliament ought to continue to represent the whole of the United Kingdom. No doubt the representatives of the National party will declare them- selves dissatisfied with any concession which falls short of the demands which they have been encouraeed to make, but if the great majority of the people of the United King- dom now distinctly and formally declare that they will give no assent to measures which will loosen the bonds of union between the two countries.and thattheyareready at the same time to give to Ireland as large a measure of self-government as is consistent with that union' it remains to be proved whether the Irish people will be persuaded to maintain a hopeless and unnecessary contest. In conclusion his Lord- ship denies that he has seceded from the principles of the Liberal party.

WARRINGTON .&ND GROUND v. - LIVBRPOOL AND 1 GROUND.—This match was played at Aigburth on Saturday.; and resulted in a victory for the home team. Warrington 1 wa.s poorly represented, while Liverpeol, in addition to snob I good men as D. Q. and F. L. Steel, Kemble and Paterson, played the two Prices and shilton: Fairclough won the toss, and sent in Wallington and J. C. Lawton. The latter was bowled at 10, and Wallington at 16. C. G. Lawton and 1 ' Denton made a stand, but Shilton was bowling too well to allow ran-getting. Clarke took Lawton'e place for three balls, and Knowles joined Denton. A fine stand was now made. Knowles bit freely, but played good cricket. His score of 27 was well received, and his play much admired. Fairclough joined Denton, but soon lost the latter, who was

THE BLeca FEVER IN *Sorrs WALES.—Black fever is said to be raging in the upper part of Rhondda Vach Val- ley. There have been 150 cases during the last fortnight, and 21 patients had already died. The epidemic has caused great alarm, and a conference of ministers, medical men, and laymen have decided that prayer meetings shall be discontinued in the, homes of all persons dying from the malady. SALMON FISHING EXTRAORDINARY.—The Chester net fishermen commenced fishing in the Dee immediately after Sunday midnight, and at eight o'clock on Monday morning some hauls of extraordinary tine fish had been taken. Two fish taken at one draught njar the old bridge at Chester weighed over 50 lbs. Toe river is closed for the whole of Sunday, and as there is no traffic the salmon have a clear run up the weir at Chester. DEATH AT A TEL MEETING.—A painful occurrence took place on Monday evening, at Newport, Mon. During the progress of an enterta*ment at the Victoria-road Con- gregational Church the daughter of the Rey. Mr. Griffiths, a Welsh minister, was observed to suddenly fall forward. She died soon after. Death was due to syncope, or failure of the heart's action. The deceased was 16 years of age, and had only just come home for the holidays from a hoard- ing school. LORD CARNARVON AND MR. PARNELL —" Truth" says :—Never was there a more damning exposure than that of Mr. Parnell in his letter to Lord Carnarvon. The Tories first made a bargain with the Irish that there should he no coercion if they would aid them in turning out a Liberal Government. The next step was to obtain the Irish vote in Great Britain. With a view to this, the Tory Viceroy of IrOand asked Mr. Parnell to meet him, and assured the Irish leader that he was in favour of the legislative inde- pendence of Ireland. No sooner, however, had the elec- tions shown that the Tories, even with the aid of the Irish, had not a Parliamentary majority, than the Tory Govern- ment veered round, denounced Home Rule, and announced Itheir intention to bring in a Coercion Act, and to oppose every species of Home Rule. Had the insidious manoeuvres of these gentlemen not succeeded in securing the Irish vote at the elections, there would have been a majority for Home Rule in Parliament at the present moment.

' NOTES BY THE WAY.

Some extraordinary cricket was witnessed at Lards on Monday in the annual match between teams representing the North and South. Though Devonport, Sugg, Brown, and Pougher batted fairly well, et remarkable stand was made when Parnbsan and White got together. They played the bowlers with ease, and were not parted until ti:ey had put on 157 runs for the last wicket. The match Australians v. Cambridge University ended in a draw. The first day's play was interfered with by the rain, and when a start did take place the Colonists kept at the wickets all day for 146 for eight wickets. The second• day's play took place under more favourable conditions. The last wicket of the Colonists was responteible for 62. When the Cantabs got to the wickets their defence was al- together too weak for the howling. Five wickets fell to Giffex before lunch for 37 runs. Afterwards Rock and Merchant made a good stand, thus saving their side from what seemed an ignominious follow on. These two raised the score from 48 to 129. On Saturday it was seen that a draw was inevitable, so that all the interest was knocked out of the game. The betting display, was however, good. It is reported that some difgculty exists about the at- *rangements for taking out a team to Australia at the end of the season. Shaw, Shrewsbury, and Lillywhite bad under- taken to take one out, and the engagement of players had been commenced, and articles in some cases signed, when, on the arrival of the present Australian team, their manager, announced that he was instructed to elect and take out a team irrespective of what Shaw and Co. might do Shaw and Shrewsbury complain. not unreasonably, that as theit contemplated visit was well known in Australia, and their arrangements and engagements for that purpose had already made considerable progress, it is hardly fair to have them upset. In last week's matches the Lancashire team showed some improvement over the previous seven days. At the Oval, in the first innings, three of the team failed to score, and eight men made 19 runs; while in the second innings seven obtained only 15 runs. Hornhy, having seen the downfall of Barlow and Dobell before a run had been scored, batted patiently, occupying an hour and a half for 31 runs. The only others to make a stand were Messrs. IL B. Steel and Watson. Surrey started badly, but subsequently W. W. Read played grandly for his 62. In Lancashire's second essay only four obtained double figures, viz., Messrs. H. B. Steel 34, Birlow 23, Pilling 16, and Dobell 15. During the game Lohmenn, who has bowled splendidly this year, got 13 wickets for 93 runs, and Watson' who was the principal bowler for Lancashire, got seven for 83 runs. It is said that there is again some friction between the Notts and the Lancashire Cricket County Clubs with refers ence to the latter county releasing two of their professionals for the metch between the Australians and Players of Eng- land at Nottingham on June 21st. The original cause of the offence arose over the North of England team at Old Trafford a fortnight age, when Notts,owing to a fixture with Sussex, could only spare two men instead of the four asked for.---" Preston Guardian." The cricket at Sheffield, on Wednesday, between York- shire and Kent, was of a most interesting description throughout. When play was resumed a draw seemed in- evitable. as Yorkshire overnight had completed an innings for 218, and Kent had lost live wickets for 186. At the close of the visitors' innines for 255, they bad an advantage of 37 runs, against which Yorkshire. on going in a second time, did so badly that six wickets were down for 67, and, with three hours left for cricket, it seemed as if Kent would win. Eventually Yorkshire, thanks to the brilliant batting of Mr. Hawke, and the valuable assistance given him by Emmett, Hunter, and Peate, succeeded in putting together 158, which left Kent 122 to get to win, but only an hour and 20 minutes to get them in. The visitors started their last innings so disastrously that five batsmen were dismissed for 23, and it appeared just poseible that Yorkshire would win after all ; but a stand by George Hearne and Mr. Thornton averted defeat, and the game was left drawn, Kent with five wickets to fall wanting 73 runs to win. In the course of less than an hour and a half's play at Old Trafford, Manchester, on Wednesday, Lancashire lost ten wickets for 58 runs, and suffered defeat at the hands of the Australians by an innings and 12 rune. The county have followed on overeight with 99 runs necessary to save the innings defeat, and 29 of this number had been obtained by Mr. Hornby and Barlow, both of whom were not out. At Nottingham, on Wednesday, the first match of the season between Notts and Surrey ended in a draw, the visit- ing county having certainly an advantage at the finish, be- ing 159 runs to the good with eight wickets to fall. As it was considered probable that the match would end in a draw, the cricket yesterday did not excite the same amount of interest that it would otherwise have done. Scotton, who was not out overnight with 51, carried his bat right through the Nottingham innings for 110. Altogether be was batting for six hours and a quarter. His figures com- ptised seven 4's, seven 3'e, thirteen 2's, and thirty-five singles.

div.head: I MR. OLADSTONE'S MANIFESTO.
div.p: I MR. OLADSTONE'S MANIFESTO.

Mr. Gladstone's address to the electors of Midlo- thian is an follows : Gentlemen--In consequence of the defeat of the Bill for the better government of Ireland, the Ministers have, advised, and her Majestry has been pleased to)sanction, a dissolution of Parliament, for the decision by the nation of the gravest, likewise the simplest, issue which has been submitted to it for half a century. It is only a sense of the gravity of this issue which induces me, at a period of life generally allowed for repose, to seek, after sitting in thirteen Parliaments, a seat in a fourteenth, and with this view to solicit the honour of your confi- dence. At the last election I endeavoured in my address and speeches to impress upon you that a great crisis had arrived in the affairs of Ireland. Weak as the late Government was for ordinary pur- poses, it had great advantages for dealing with this crisis. A comprehensive measure proceeding from them would have reoeived warm and extensive sup- port from within the Liberal party. It would probably have closed the Irish controversy within the pre- sent session, and have left the Parliament of 1885 free to prosecute the now stagnant work of ordin- ary legislation with the multitude of questions that it includes. My earnest hope was to support the late Cabinet in such a course of conduct. But on the 26th of last January the opposite policy of coercion Was declared to have been the choice of the Government, Lord Carnarvon alone refusing to share in it. The Irish question was thus placed in the foreground to the exclusion of every other. The hour, as all felt, was come, and the only point remaining to be determined was the manner in which it should be dealt With. In my judgment the proposal of coercion was not justified by the facts, and was condemned to a certain and dis- graceful failure. Some method of governing Ire- land other than coercion ought, as I thought, to be sought for, and might be found. I, therefore, viewed without regret the fall of the late Cabinet, and when summoned by her Majesty to form a new one, I undertook it with the basis of an anti-coer- cion policy 4 with a full explanation to those whose aid 1 sought as colleagues, that I proposed to examine whether it would not be possible to grant to Ireland a domestic legislature under conditions such as to Maintain the honour and consolidate the unity of the empire. The Cabinet was formed, and the work was at once put in hand. You will now, gentlemen, clearly understand how and why it is that the affairs of Ireland have, not for the first time, thrust aside every other subject, and adjourned our hopes of useful and progressive legislation. As a question of the first necessity of social order, it forced itself into the van. The late Government, right in giving it that place, were, as we thought, wrong in their manner of treating it. It was our absolute duty on taking the Government, if we did not adopt their method to propose another. Thus, gentlemen, it is that this great and simple issue has come upon you, and demands your deci- sion. Will you govern Ireland by coercion, or will you let her manage her own affairs? To debate in this address this or that detail of the lately defeated bill would be only to disguise this issue, and would be as futile as to discuss the halting, stumbling, ever- shifting, ever-vanishing projects of the intermediate class, which is proposed from seceding Liberals. Two clear, positive, intelligible plans are before the world. There is a plan of the Government, and there is a plan of Lord Salisbury. Our plan is ,that Ireland should, under well-considered conditions, transact her own affairs.. His plan is to ask Parlia- ment far new repressive measures, and to enforce them resolutely for 20 years, at the end of which time, he assures us, lrelan4 will be fit to accept any gifts in the way of local government, or the repeal of coercion laws, that you may wish to give her. I leave this daring project to speak for itself in its un- adorned simplicity, and; I turn to the proposed policy of the Government. • Our opponents, gentlemen, whether Tories or se- ceders, have assumed the name of Unionists. I deny their title to if, In intention, incl And, ,we a,re 01 UlliOntsts all 6, but the L'illon 'which they refuse to modify is in its present shape a paper union ob- tained by force and fraud, and never sanctioned or accepted by the Irish nation. They are not union- ists, but paper unionists. True union is to be tes- ted by the sentiment of human beings united. Tried by this Criterion, we have less union between Great Britain and Ireland now than we had under the settlement of 1782. Enfranchised Ireland, gentle- men, asks through her lawful representatives for a revival of her domestic Legislature, not on the face of it an innovative but a restmative proposal. She urges with truth that the centralisation of the Par- liaments has been the division of the peoples, but she recognises the fact that the Union, lawlessly as it was obtained, cannot and ought not to be re- pealed. She is content to receive her Legislature in a form divested of prerogatives which might have impaired Imperial interests, and better adap- ted than the settlement of 1782 to secure to her regular control of her own affairs. She has not re- pelled but has welcomed stipulations for the pro- tection of the minority. To such provisions we have given, and shall give careful heed; but I trust that Scotland condemn the attempts so singu- larly made to import into this controversy the veno- mous element of religious bigotry. Let us take warning from the deplorable riots of Belfast, and some other places in the north. Among the benefits, gentlemen, which I antici- pate from your acceptance of our policy, are these: —The consolidation of the unity of the empire, and a great addition to its strength; the,stoppage of the heavy, constant, and demoralising waste of public treasure; the abatement and gradual extinction of ignoble feuds in Ireland, and the development of her resources, which experience shows to be the natural consequence of free, and orderly govern- ment; the redemption of the honour of Great Bri- tain from a stigma fastened upon her almost from time immemorial in respect•to Ireland by the judg- ment of the whole civilised world, and lastly the restoration of Parliament to its' dignity, efficiency, and the regular progress of the business of the country. Well, gentlemen, the first question now put to you is, hew shall Ireland be governed; and there is another behind it and involved in it—how are Eng- land and Scotland to be governed? 'You know haw, for the last six years especially, the affairs of Eng- land and Scotland have been impeded, and your Im- perial Parliament discredited and disabled. All this happened while Nationalists were but a small majority of Irish members without the support of so much as a handful of members not Irish. Now they approach 90, and are entitled to say we speak the voice of the Irish nation. It is impossible to deal with this subject by half measures. They are strong in numbers, strong in the British support, which has brought 313 members to vote • for their country., and strongest of all in the sense of being right. But we have done our part. The rest re- mains with you, the electors of the country. May you be enabled to see through and to cast away ail delusions, to refuse the evil and to choose the good. I have the honour to be, gentlemen, your most faith- ful and grateful servant, W. E. GLADSTON.E. 10, Downing-street, 12th June, 1886.

SERIOUS ILLNESS OF THE REV. CANON CARE. A general feeling of sorrow has been manifested at the an- nouncement that the Rev. Edward Carr. LL.D., Canon of Liverpool, who has been vicar of St. Helens for forty year?, has for about a week past been seriously ill at his residence. Denton'-green. On Triursday week the venerable gentle- man, who is eighty years of age and has been in feeble health for some years past, officiated at the funeral of the Rev. R. P. Crockett, 8.A., who had been ticar of Christ Church, Eccleston, for forty-eight years. After the inter- ment Canon Carr was taken ill, and en the following morn- ing was seized with paralysis, which affected the right side of his head and body. Dr. Twyford, :LP., his medical ad- viser, was promply in attendance, and although the gravest fears were entertained that the rev. gentleman could not rally, the suspence of his family and friends was an Sunday night relieved by his partially recovering consciousness,. and speaking to those near him. THE 2 ST L.R.V. (ST. HELENS) AT SOUTIIPORT.— For the first time in the history of the corps the 21st L.R.V. have this year encamped away from St. Helens, and chosen Southport for their outing. The advance party, consisting of Quartermaster-Sergeant Wallis, two sergeant-instructors, and twelve men, proceeded on Tuesday, and when the main body reached Southport late on Friday night, everything was in readiness for them. The men who arrived in camp comprised 15 officers, 22 sergeants. and 309 rank and file. They marched to their camp headed by their band, and were followed on Saturd-y by seven sergeants and 47 men. A few of the men are only stopping in camp for three days, but en Monday there were fresh arrivals to fill their places. The officer in camp are Col. W. W. Pilkingten, Majors Bramwell, White, Windus, and 14.1‘Tear ; Captain and Acting Adjutant Brumner, Captain Dickinson, Limits. Woifenden, Cooke, Gossage, Mho. D. Gamble, Lewis, Hall, and Thom- son; Surgeons it. Wisticoll and Gasket% ; Quartermaster- Sergeant Balshaw, and Sergeant-Major Tyson. There are put up on the ground two marquees and 101 tents. On Sunday morning a Church of England service was held on the ground at half-past ten,' while those of the otnan Catholic persuasion attended St. Marie's Chapel in Seabank- road. The camp will be broken up to-lay (Friday). Orders have been received from the War-office that the title of the regiment is to be altered from the 21st to the 2nd Volunteer Battalion Prince of Wales Volunteers.

div.head: TRE MIDLOTHIAN CAMPAIGN.
div.p: TRE MIDLOTHIAN CAMPAIGN.

The annual meeting of the Midlothian Liberal As- sociation was held in Edinburgh on Wednesday aftern.oon,. Mr. Cowan presiding. A letter was read. from Lord Rosebery saying he was sure the Associa- tion would remain true to theirchoice of Mr. Glad- stone; otherwise they would cease to represent the popular feeling- of Midlothian. Lord Dalhousie moved. a resolution of confidence in Mr. Gladstone and ap- proval of his Irish policy, which was carried by 51), votes to 14.

The opposition threatened to Mr. Gladstone by Colonel Campbell Walker is not regarded as a-serious matter, and the probability is that the Colonel's in- tervention is regarded by the Conservatives as an embarrassment rather than an advantage, Nor have the anti-Ministerialists derived much encourage- ment from the proceedings of the Midlothian Liberal Association. The anti-Government men,

though well organised, could not number more than rl4 against 51, although it was noticeable that a number of delegates did not vote. It should be re- membered that the most prominent man in the ranks of the seceders, Sir John Don Wauchope, sup- ported Lord Dalkeith against Mr. Gladstone in 1880.. The Liberal opposition to the Prime Minister in, Midlothian cannot therefore count much, and will furnish a very slender reinforcement to the Tory party so signally defeated last November. MR. GLADSTONE'S JOURNEY.—ENTHUSIASTIC

div.head: RECEPTION.
div.p: RECEPTION.

Mr. Gladstone started upon his Midlothian cam- paign on Thursday morning. The Prime Minister rose early, and at nine o'clock he joined Mr. Prim- rose, his private secretary, in his study, where he remained busily engaged until a quarter to ten o'clock. He appeared quiteivelland full of vigour. At a few minutes after ten he emerged from his resid- ence, and took his seat in the carriage with Mrs.Glad- stone,amid cheers,which h e frequ en tly ac k nowie dged. Mr. Gladstone wore a silk hat and a mixed suit of tweed manufacture; lie also had on an Inverness cape of a dark mixture cloth. The carriages then drove from Downing-street to St. Pancras Station. As the carriage reached the station loud cheers were raised by large cro.wds both outside and inside. Thousands of people lined both sides of the road- way, and so great was the crush that the progress of the carriage was, somewhat impeded. The crowd followed the carriage into the station and on to the platform, where there were already assembled a large number of persons, and the new arrivals in their impetuosity swept away the improvised bar- riers. Mr. Gladstone had some difficulty in reaching his carriage, so excited and enthusiastic was the crowd which surrounded him, and he had, in fact, to stop several times to acknowledge the warmness of the greetings of his admirers. A cordon of police was drawn up around the carriage, but the crowd pressed round and clamoured loudly for a speech.

div.head: DEPARTING MESSAGE TO TEE METROPOLIS.
div.p: DEPARTING MESSAGE TO TEE METROPOLIS.

In response, therefore, to these appeals, Mr. Gladstone said :—Gentlemen, I cannot depart from London without thanking you, and thanking then- sands more who are not within hearing, for this extraordinary display of enthusiasm. (Cheers.) What is the cause of this enthusiasm? It is because we feel that we are engaged in a great, noble, national, and imperial undertaking. (Cheers.) What is the reason, gentlemen, of all this excite- ment, and of the present dissolution? (Cheers and some groans.) It is because the people of Ireland want to manage their own affairs, and want to cease fTom giving trouble to you and to themselves. (Cheers.) Why are they prevented from doing s)? Our opponents say that it is because they are a nation unworthy to be trusted. Ido not believe God has made any one of the nations unworthy to be trusted. Your opponents say that Canada is. worthy to be trusted, that the 'people of Australia are worthy to be trusted, but that the people of Ireland cannot be trusted. The ques- tion which you and your brother eleeter* out the country have to detz-rmine, the alternative that is before tltzz, is whether you will govern Irelqn4 .of ttnildence or by force. That is the uetioil fore the country, Do not allow it to be, taken from you by any subterfuge. But say yes or- no to it. (Cheers.) I wish you the greatest happi- ness and the greatest prosperity as citizens of the greatest empire in the world. The right hon. gentleman concluded his remarks at 10,35 amid repeated burst A of applause. The whistle immediately sounded, and,the train slowly glided out of the station. Mr. Gladstone stood at the window and bowed his, acknowledgments to the large body of spectators as cheer after cheer arose. The applause did not subside until the 'whole train had left the station on its way to the North. Just before the train left the sun burst forth, adding to the brilliance of the demonstration.

About 10,000 people had collected at Leicester,. and awaited in the station yard the arrival of the train in which the Premier was travelling. It was with great difficulty that Ur. T. T. Paget, M.P., (who, with Mr. Ellis, M.P., was to have introduced a Liberal deputation to the Premier), could reach the right hon. gentleman. The excitement was intense, but after some delay addresses were presented from the local Liberals, and the • Premier, in response, said :—lt is impossible to make .myself audible to the vast enthusiastic body of persons here assembled. I ' must thank you for the ad- dresses which you have been good enough to present to me. In two of those addresses it is remarked with great justice that Leicester is an ancient stronghold of Liberal principles. About that matter there can be no doubt whatever, and. therefore to bring Liberal principles to Leicester, is exactly like bringing coals to Newcastle. I don't come here for such a purpose, and time forbids me to enter on the great question now before the coun- try—namely, whether you will give the people of Ireland that which you have given with the greatest advantage to the people of your colonies the power to manage not Imperial but Irish affairs. I will only tell you of two things, one that after fifty-four years of public life I have 'never witnessed such enthuSiasm as exists in all places where I have been in this great cause, and the second is that the eyes of the world are now upon you in a degree in which they have never been before directed towards this country. At Trent junction Mr. Gladstone received a bou- quet and an address brought by a deputation from the Primitive Methodist Conference sitting at Derby. Replying to this address, the right hon. gentleman expressed his gratification at finding that the sub- scribers to it were deliberately set upon complying with tub reasonable, determined, a,nd traditional de- sires of their fellow subjects in/ Ireland. At Nor- manton an enthusiastic Scotch admirer presented. a hazel stick bearing an inscription which inclu- ded a suggestion that it was "to thrash de- serting Whigs and Liberals with." Here also several addresses were presented. In his reply to them Mr. Gladstone remarked that if at the last election the rest of the country had folloWed the example of Yorkshire he should not then be on his way to Midlothian. The next presentation of an address was at Skipton, and the reply recognised the fact that the further the train got north the greater and the more abundant the fervour became. In a short reply to an address at Carlisle the Prime Minister referred to the Carnarvon-Parnell contro- versy. He said it was unfortunate that while Lord Carnarvon had told them what he did not _ say, he had not told them what he did say; ansi 'while he had told themi that he did not communi- cate his conversation with Mr. Parnell to the Cabi- net, ho had not told them who he did communicate it to. He would ask Lord Carnarvon two questions —What did he say to Mr. Parnell, and to whom did he make known his conversation? Knowing some- thing of the relations between members of Cabinets,. he was able to say that it would have been an act of treachery on the part of Lord. Carnarvon if he held such a conversation' with Mr. Parnell and had not made it known to Lord Salisbury. It was the right of the nation that. they should know 'exactly what took place between the late Government and the Nationalists, and it would not be his fault if they did not come to know what actually did take place. The Premier's re- ception in Edinburgh was a magnificent one. Thousands of people lined the streets, and an im- mense crowd escorted the right hon. gentleman to his hotel, where he appeared for a few minutes on the balcony, but made no effort to speak. After- wards the crowd held a meeting on Calton Hill, and a resolution in favour of Home Rule was submitted and carried with enthusiasm.

A fire broke out on Tuesday at Elmhill Lunatic Asylum, Aberdeen. Twenty-six male patients were occupying the apartment, but they were all removed in safety. One man, however, escaped and is still at large. &focus° Dixrit.—William 31cEwen. forty-five years of age, who lived with his wife at 68, Iligby-streist., St. Helens, met with a shocking dcath at the Orrell Fite Clay Works, near Wigan, on Friday last. Dummied was a foreman brickmakor, and was in charge of the machinery. The knives of a brick machine were not working properly., sad he went ap to the top with a spade to remove the ob. struotion. Whilst doing so he was caught by the cog- wbeela and dragged in, with the result that be was fear- fully crushed and instantty killed.. The body was brought home te 13,.. Holm on Sunday night.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, JUNE 19, 1886.

THE Addresses of both candidates for the honour of representing Warrington in the , hext Parliament are before the electors; and i the fullest preparations are being made for a ; conflict which if short will certainly be sharp, Air. JOHN CROSFIELD'S Address is eminently characteristic ; it is clear, pointed, and straightforward. He relies upon his political • opiniorts being well known from the fact of his having for five and thirty years "taken a , Warm interest in promoting the principles of 1 the Liberal party.' s: Peace, Retrenchment, i and Reform" are, for him, the watchwords of 1 the future as they have been his watchwords: in the past. He is amongst those who think ; that nations are too ready .to use the sword as ' a weapon rather than the pen; and, while ! anxious to promote the trade and commerce ' Of the empire, he believes that this is best ' accomplished by recognising that "the 1 greatest of British interests is peace." He is 1 in favour of " perfect religious freedom and equality ; " and is a supporter of "the volun- tary and denominational school system." We ! are not ourselves enamoured of the existing ; sYstem of Naional Education; but we can give and take in a matter of this kind, especially as the question is one which be- i longs, as things go, to "the dim and distant future." The one issue which at the present I inoment over-rides every other is Mr. GLAD: STONE'S measure of Home Rule for Ireland, With regard to which Mr. CROSFIELD Suc- cinctly and pointedly says to the electors— , You will have to decide at the Polling Booths , bether you are in favour of giving to the Irish I -lotion a Domestic Legislature under conditions Such as to maintain the honour and consolidate the Unity of the Empire, or whether you will support Lord Salisbury's policy of Twenty Years more of i Coercion, and the banishment from the land of their , birth of another million of Irishmen at a cost of I Fifty -Million Pounds Sterling. The Tories are not a little annoyed in War- rington and elsewnere at the issue being thus nakedly placed before the electors. It is stated that Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL is by no means pleased with Lord SALISBURY for having committed himself out and out to a policy of repression. Local Conservatives feel the same difficulty; and Dr. MACKIE Went the length, on Tuesday evening, of say- ing that "the charge made against Lord SALISBURY that he spoke of twenty years" coercion as being the remedy for the diseased state of Ireland was foul in the extreme." As the Neutral Editor, who speaks so one-sidedly, did not dare to quote Lord SALISBURY, we Will, at the risk of repetition, do it for him. Ills Lordship, speaking at St. James's Hall, said ;—" The alternative policy is that Par- liament should enable the Government of England to govern Ireland. Apply that re- cipe honestly, consistently, and resolutely for twenty years, and at the end of that time you will find Ireland will be fit to accept any gifts in the way of local self-government or repeal of coercion laws." Foul or fine, the word " coercion" is not put into Lord SALISBURY'S Mouth; it is taken from it. If he means something else when he says "coercion," let him explain, and explain again, and—we will try to believe him. Mr. CROSFIELD is fully Justified in speaking. of Lord SALISBURY'S Policy as one of "• Twenty Years more of Coercion ;". for even if there had been a I Slip of the tongue on the part of the leader of ' the Tory party, there is the fact that on the 26th of January last Sir MICHAEL HICKS- tEACH announced that the policy which the then (Tory) Government intended to pursue ti Was that of "the suppression of the National League." If that is not a policy of coercion, Will Dr. MACKIE, or some other Neutral, say . What is? Sir GILBERT GREENALL'S Address is short, but it cannot be said to be sweet. The state- //lent that he will "resist the proposed legis- lative separation of Ireland from Great Britain " will be as a sour crab, if not Dead Sea fruit, to the Irishmen who voted for him at the last election. Legislative separation the grant to Ireland, as Mr. GLADSTONS has it, of "a Domestic Legislature "—is pre- cisely what Irishmen are struggling for, and it is precisely what Sir GILBERT GREENALL says he will " resist." He has not " changed colours "—not a bit of it; they ought to have known that when he was patting "my friend, JOHN ROBERTS," the Orangeman, on the back, he had as little regard for Irishmen and , Catholics as he had when opposing the
A

Maynooth Grant; or voting in favour of Mr. Newdegate's motion for the public inspection of Convents: or voting on Tuesday morning week against Home Rule for Ireland. It is true that "the Old Obadiah" —to pre- serve one of the MAYOR'S quaint phrases— talks in a vague and general way about "autonomy in domestic matters;" but then we have it on the authority of "the Young Obadiah" that this is a species of literary thimble-rigging which cannot be too strongly condemned. Speaking at the Caucus Meet- ing in the Tory Club on Tuesday evening, Mr. ROBERT PIERPOINT "asked those pre- sent not to be deceived by names. He did not like such useless Greek words as auto- nomy." This remark was received with laughter, connected as it was with a reference to Mr. GLADSTONE ; but it oddly happens that the word " autonomy " is not used in either the PRIME MINISTER'S Manifesto or in MT. CROSFIELD'S Address. We must look to the Address of the Walton octogenarian for such "useless Greek words as autonomy ;" and, like Mr. ROBERT PIERPOINT, make up our minds "not to be deceived by names." There was deception enough, Heaven knows, at the last Election; Irishmen have in'this respect a great wrong to redress; and if they are alive, as we believe they are, to their true interests—to • the tremendous stake which they have in the next Election—they will rise to the height of the occasion, and sweep the halting, mumbling GREENALLS of politics from the Parliamentary board.

MR. GLADSTONE'S triumphal progress to Scotland demonstrates the truth of the statement we made last week—namely, that the country is riper on the question of Home Rule than the House of Commons. As for Edinburgh itself, it may be said, in the language of our great poet, that "the city cast its people out upon him." It is significant that before he left London—for London is bad to stir—there was an outburst of enthusiasm. The cheering crowd de- manded a word from • him, and, responding, he stated, briefly and simply, the issue ' which is before the nation. "What," he said, " is the reason of this excitement and of the present dissolution ? It is because the people of Ireland want to manage their own affairs, and want to cease from giv- ing, trouble to you and to themselves. And why are they not permitted to do it ? It is because our opponents hold that that nation is unworthy to be trusted. Now, gentlemen, I don't believe that God has made any one of these three nations un- worthy to be trusted." At Carlisle, the PRIME MINISTER referred to the interview between Lord CARNARVON and Mr. PARNELL, and to the alleged promise that the Conserva- tives "might give to Ireland a domestic legis- lature with the power of imposing protective duties." He does not deem it sufficient to let the matter rest where it stands ; he is resolved to get at the truth, and the whole truth, and the nation will applaud him in this determination. There is no escape from the demand which Mr. GLADSTONE thus makes : _ _

Now I wish to put these two questions to Lord Carnarvon : "What did you say to Mr. Parnell, and to whom did you make known your conversation with Mr. Parnell?" (Cheers.) I know perfectly well that Lord Carnarvon must, if he knew his duty as a Cabinet Minister, have made known that conversation to Lord Salisbury. He had no right— I tell you this, it is forty years since I entered the Cabinet—l have sat in seven Cabinets, and I know something by this time of the relations between members of Cabinets, and I say it would have been treachery on the part of Lord Carnarvon—i should be the last to accuse him of it—if he held such a conversation as that with a person in the position of Mr. Parnell, and had not made it known to Lord Salisbury. (Cheers.) I say, therefore, publicly, that, until it is denied by him, I should be perfectly sure that he did his duty by making known to Lord Salisbury the conversation. (Loud cheers.) Neither Lord SALISBURY nor Lord CARNAR- VON can afford to ignore the demand for an explanation made in this public manner by the Prime Minister of England. The electors are about to be asked to decide as to the best course to be taken in settling the Irish question; and they have a right to know, before coming to a decision, how far st ites- men, who now denounce Home Rule, have committed themselves in the past in bargain- ing with Home Rulers.

, The Liberals of St. Helens are entering upon the Election Campaign with enthusi- asm, having good hopes, now that the Irish ,1 electors have returned to their allegiance, of I reversing the defeat which they sustained in November last. Colonel GAMBLE, much to the regret of the majority of the inhabitants, finds himself unable to consent to be nomi- nated as the Liberal candidate; but he does not stand in the way of anyone else. On the contrary, he is doing all he can to ensure the su:cess of Mr. ARTHUR SINCLAIR, J.P., the final choice of the Liberal Six Hundred. Mr. Sinclair is especially fitted from a varied busi- ness experience extending over forty years to represent a thriving commercial community like that of St. Helens. He knows the needs of the town as well as any gentleman in it. He is not a stranger to the place, for he was one of the Commissioners for St Helens as far back as 1847. It is worthy of note, too, that he was one of the most prominent workers for Mr. GLADSTONE in 1868, and that it was to Mr. SINCLAIR that Lord DERBY first intimated that he had resolved to take his stand on a Liberal platform. Colonel GAMBLE, as a member of the firm with which Mr. SINCLAIR is connected can speak from long experience and positive knowledge, and he was very emphatic at the meeting the other night in declaring that there were few men either in the House of Commons or out of it who had such a close knowledge of the history of the House of Commons for the past fifty years. All this goes to show that the new candidate is no novice; that he is leaping where he as sown: and that if he Is returned to Parliament the people of St. Helens will have in him a representative who will be recognised as a progressive Liberal whilst supporting the greatest statesman of of the age in giving justice to Ireland.

THE SHIP CANAL MONEY BILL.-011 Friday the Select Committee of the Lords on the Mauchester Ship Canal Money Bill (Earl Milltown in the chair), after a lengthy argument, allowed the locus of the Dock Board and the Corporation of Liverpool to be heard on the merits of the bill. The London and North-Western Railway Company did not appear upon their petition. PENKETH WESLEYAN CHAPEL.—On Sunday the anniversary sermons in connection with the Wes- leyan Sunday School, were preached in the morn- ing by the Rev. G. E. Cutting, of Warrington, from Proverbs, cap. 23, verse 23, and in the evening the Rev. J. Yonge, Warrington, occupied the pulpit and preached from Revelations, chap. 3, verse 4. In the afternoon a service of song entitled "The de- sire of all nations" was rendered by a trained choir of elder scholars, teachers, etc., in a most creditable and worthy manner. The sermons were highly ap- preciated by a large and appreciative audience. Mr. James Watson was the conductor, . and Miss lichen ' Garnett acted as organist. Various hymns were sung morning and evening by the children. The collections amounted to £lB 2* for the day.
"TOUCH AND GO."
hope and the Irish with enthusiasm; he is a Grand Old Man!
" Light ! more light ! " was the street cry in Warrington last night. Where were the lamplighters? Were they deliberately let- ting the thieves have a sort of holiday time of it?
Mr. Argustine Birrill is to be the Liberal candidate for the Widnes Division. He is a Gladstonian Home Ruler, a sound Liberal, and a good speaker. He should win in a canter.
It is stated that Mr. William Crosfield, J•P.. will be invited to become the Liberal candidate for Anglesey. We trust this is true; he would be an honour to any con- stituency.
It is a matter of course that Mr. Brunner, M.P., will be seleated for the Northwich Divi- sion. The Tories have not the slightest chance of being able to beat him, and they are very unhappy.

The Newton Rifle Volunt-ers are men of mark as marksmen; the local squad has again carried off the shield, at Altcar, in the an- nual prize competition of the i9th L.R.V. (Liverpool Press Guards). Let us hope that they will always be in a position to "kill at so° yards," and never have occasion to try.

Sir George Errington will, in all proba- bility, be the Liberal candidate for Newton, strongly recommended, as he is, by the Ex- ecutive. There is a large number of Catholics in the Division who will be delighted at this tribute to a member of their faith. and as Sir George is, above all, a staunch Liberal and a loyal supporter of Mr. Gladstone, he will be acceptable to the Liberal party.

The public of St. Helens are now possessed of a Park "to have and to hold for ever- more," what has been known as the Cowley Hill estate being formally dedicated to the inhabitants on Monday last. It is fortunate for the ratepayers that they have got a Park "ready made and a good fit." What with the lengthening of chimneys, and the breath- ing space now afforded, St. Helens is im- proving. If Mr. Mathew Arnold will pay it a visit during one of the three fine days which constitute our summer, ht will see some- thing in the way of sweetness and light.

"Vote for Greenall and good wages"—that was the cry at the last election, and on the strength of it the Sankey wire-workers marched to the poll in a body. They had their reward; it came in the shape of Paddy's rise—a big reduction ; and now they "make remarks" when anything is said about " Greenall and good wages."

Captain Reynolds, as the leader of the Conservative host, would of course know all about the placarded promise of" good wages;" and it would be interesting to ascertain whether he has convinced the tanners whose wages he has reduced that the promise has been faithfully kept. Perhaps on the old Tory theory that the masses should be kept down, the leaders of the Tory party in War- rington think that /ow wages are "good wages." Had they not better explain, and before the polling day?

The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, of Warring- ton, has resumed his old occupation as a fisher of men on behalf of the Tory party. He has conceived a sudden affection for Liberals of a certain, or rather uncertain class, and he has the "greatest respect," he says, for Nonconformists—who go wrong. He is an artful angler, doubt, and has some nice new bait; but the Liberal fish know the Carleton hook; they won't bite.

Sir Gilbert Greenall is trying, politically speaking, to sit on the fence; he will resist " legisla:ive separation," and yet he is in favour of" autonomy in domestic matters " whatever that may mean. He tried "sitting on alp fence," literally, at the Ironworks Sports on Saturday, and came to grief. It was an omen ; he will come to grief with the other fence before he is many weeks older. Greenall's " wearing of the green,"
It will nevermore be seen; For his Home Rule vote has brought him in dis- grace. Though he turn and turn about, Ireland's sons have found him out, And they mean to put John Crosfield in his place.

Mr. Robert Davies thinks it would be a good thing for Mr. John Crosfield to stay at home and perfect his " Perfection" soap. Pity, with regard to the trades of the candi- dates, that the compliment cannot be re- turned. Soap, as related to cleanliness, cannot be far from godliness ; but the "common brewer" is unfortunately not un- commonly regarded as belonging to "the devil's own."

It is suggestive that Sir Robert Peel, a Tory, should resign a safe seat at Blackburn because of his conversion to Home Rule. Sir Robert has always been erratic as a politician; but it is worth remembering that, like Lord Carnarvon, who is also, in principle, a Home Ruler, he has had official experience of government in Ireland. With these men, an ounce of experience is of more value than a ton of theory.

Mr. Chamberlain. after changing his ground a time or two, harks back to his local self- government proposals for Great Britain and Ireland. He shuts his eyes to the fact that, so far as Ireland is concerned, his scheme got the quielus when the Tories entered into an alliance with the Parnellites previous to the last election. Perhaps he has ceased to read the papers, or he would surely have seen something of the accounts of the memorable interview between the Tory Lord Lieutenant of Ireland and the leader of the Irish Nation- alists.

And what does Mr. Chamberlain mean by speaking of Mr. Gladstone's Land Bill as a ‘gigantic bribe?" Does he think Mr. Glad- stone capable of bribing anybody? We gave Mr. Chamberlain credit for being above using the vulgar slang of platform rowdies of the Churchill type. He would be the first to resent—and would justly resent—;any refer- ence to his land allotment scheme, or free education proposals, as bribes—gigantic or otherwise. Let him do as he would be done by.

Mr. Gladstone's Manifesto is in his best vein—both as to matter and manner. There is no picking holes in it. And with what ease the cobwebs of sophistry are brushed aside! He leaves Lord Hartington untouched and alone in his helplessness; he pins Lord Salisbury down .to his alternative policy of coercion; and airily dismisses Mr. Chamber- -lain as the fertile but futile author of" halt- ing, stumbling, ever shifting, ever vanishing projects." He inspires the English with

THE GENERAL ELECTION.—LIST OF CANDIDATES. I—The Central News has issued a list of the candi- dates now before the constituencies. From this it appears that. there is a total of 325 Gladstonian Liberals, 115 Unionists, and 380 Conservatives 'be- fore the electors in Great Britain. In 33 instances Gladstonian Liberals are opposed by Liberal Union- ists, and in 187 cases by Conservatives. That it will be next to impossible to restrain a conflict in all constituencies between Liberal Unionists and Conservatives is shown by the fact that in 18 divi- sions both Liberal Unionist and Conservative candi- dates are at present before the electors. A feature of the coming election will be the large number of seats which will be uncontested, there being no fewer than 292 places where, up to the present, only one candidate is in the field. Of these candi- dates 78 are Gladstonians, 58 are Unionists, and 156 are Conservatives. Although this number will be considerably reduced before the nomination day, the majority of these seats will probably be nn- contested. The clubs moved through the principal thorough- fares of the town, and then proceeded to Halton, where they made a brief stay. Meadowcroft. the Run- corn agent to the Company; and Messrs. J. Littler T. Simister, R. Rawlinson, J. K. Digges, and T. Done. After marching through the town the procession proceeded to the vicarage, and returning to the Parish Church, took part in divine service. The festival of the schools took place in the afternoon At the appointed time, the weather was so bad that it was thought no demonstration would take place, but the children braved the elements, and their procession through the town was watched with interest by a large number of spectators. Conforming to custom, the Nonconformists Sunday schools held a united demonstratien. They marched in the follow- ing order :—Brunswick. 536 scholars; St. John's, 201 ; Be- thesda, 118; St. Luke's' 111 ; Primitive Methodists, 261 ; Mill Brow, 33; United Methodist Free Church, 141; Cam- den, 384; Neleon-street, 110; Mersey Missions, 370. The total number in the proceeshin as shown by the above-men- tioned figures was 2,605 ; and with banners waving, and bands playing, they made a good show. The procession was admirably marshalled by Mr. J. W. Woodland. It had been arranged that the children should spend the afternoon in a field off Heath-road, but in consequence of the rain this part of the programme bad to be abandoned. In con- sequence the time was spent in the schoolroom in a variety of games, and was followed by a tea. In the evening enter- tainments were held. Na procession was organised in con- nection with the F-yer-street Ragged School on account of many of the children being insufficiently clothed. The scholars were, however, treated to a tea party and entertain- ment in the evening. The children attending the schools of the Established Church were entertained at their respective schools. At the National School 780 children assembled, including those connected with the Newtown Mission, but the procession was abandoned, and the afternoon was rpent enjoyably in- doors. Later in the afternoon, however, a number of the elder scholars walked to the vicarage headed by the Widnes Soap Works Band. The Scholars of the Holy Trinity Church paraded the town in processional order, and after- wards returned to the schools, where they were wrovided with tea. An entertainment followed. Chadwick, ; J.P , where the band in connection with the school dis- coursed several selections of music. A cad was also made at the vicarage. On returning to the mission room, each child was presented with a bun and an orange. The Wes- leyan scholars also paraded through the village, and were afterwards entertained to tea. NORITIWICII DIVISION. II To-day the Liberal Council for the ..Northwich Division meets at Winsford to formally select their candidate. Mr. Brunner, ALP., will be present and deliver a speech, and it is not expected that there will be any opposition to his adoption as the Liberal ! champion at the impending election. There ,is ; great probability that Mr. Robert Verdin will come forward as a Liberal Unionist candidate, and that the Conservatives, in preference to running a can- didate of their own in the person of his brother, Mr. ;W. 11. Verdin, will give him their support. The General Committee of the Conservatives meets to- day at Northwich to consider what action they I shall take.
A LIBERAL CANDIDATE FOR WIDNES.

Last night a meeting of the Widnes District Liberal Council was held in Lacey-street School for the purpose of considering the recommendation by the Executive Council that Mr. Augustine Birrell be the Liberal candidate for the Widnes Division. Mr. E. Carey presided over the proceedings, which passed. off in a most cordial man- ner. Mr. Buren, it was stated, was a Home Ruler and a staunch supporter of Mr. Glad- stone's Irish policy. The meeting, however, did not confine its attention merely to his Irish views. Numerous questions were asked as to his opinions upon other political matters which the Liberal party desire to see dealt with. They were satisfac- torily answered by reading extracts from the ad- dress published to the Walton (Liverpool) electors last November by Mr. Birrell, who was the candidate for that division on that occasion. Additional information was given by the chairman, who had had an interview,with the proposed can- didate, and elicited his opinions upon other subject§ which, though at present overshadowed by Houfi; Rule, are certain to come to the front before long. A draft address to the Widnes constituency, written by Mr. Birrell, with a view to his selection, was read, and met with the hearty ap- proval of those present.—lt was then unanimously decided, on the motion of Mr. F. Heyes, seconded by Mr. F. Cane, that Mr. Birrell should contest the constituency. Simultaneously with this meeting, the councils of Garston, Woolton, and Huyton met to consider . the same subject, and a similar •result of the pro- ceedings was confidently anticipated. ! Mr. Birrell, it may be stated, is a native of Liver- pool and son of the Rev. Mr. Birrell, who was for 25 years the minister of Pembroke Baptist Chapel.. He ;is a sound Liberal and a capital speaker, and will ! no doubt conduct the campaign, which will be com- menced at once, to asuccessful issue. His opponent ! will be thepresent member, Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss. llt is probable Mr. Birrell will address the Widnes electors on Tuesday evening next; and that dur- ing next week Mr. Moss will adaress his con- stituents.
