NARROW ESCAPE FROM DROWNING IT WIDNES.—On Thursday, whilst playing with a ball on the flat Llanfair, now lying in West Bank Dock, Maggie (Thiel, daughter of the captain of the boat, and Kate McCafferty, daughter of James McCafferty, who lives at Newtown, fell into the water. The girls screamed loudly, and a youth employed on the Slat William and Alice, jumped into a small boat and rowed towards them. He succeeded in rescuing both the girls, who were in an exhausted condition, ard must have inevitably been drowned but for his timely aid. TREATING WIDNES MAGISTRATES WITH CONTEMPT.— At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday. Richard Tenkies, a youth with a wooden leg, was charged with obstructing the footpath. P,C. Marshall said when he gave the defend- ant (who did not appear) the summons, he cursed him, and said he should not attend. On Sunday afternoon the de- fendant was lying on his back on the footpath in Church. street, and many people had to go into the roadway in con- sequence. When requested to move he was very insolent, and did not get up until threatened with imprisonment. The defendant, who is not a stranger to the pblice court, was fined 108 and costs. HALTON WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL.—Tite scholars of this school had their annual demonstration on Whit Mon- day. Despite the wet weather, the children met at the school at two o'clock, and paraded the village in proces- sional order. It had been arranged to spend the afternoon in a field lent by Mr. William Nixon, but on acceunt of the rain the children went to the school, where tea was pro- vided. The scholars were accompanied by the Rev. A. P. Watson and Messrs. Hugh Rowe, sen., Joseph Astbury' and J. H. Gamon, superintendents. Total number of scholars on the rolls-117 males, 129 females; average afternoen at- tendance, 142; number of teachers, 18 males and 8 females. Number of books in library, 396. WIFE DESERTION AT WIDNES.—OD Thursday, at Wid- nes Petty Sessions, Thomas Woolley, alias Wm. Davies, appeared on remand charged with deserting his wife and child who were chargeable to the common fund of the Prescot Union. Mr. Scannell, relieving officer, said on the 30th May the prisoner had a child dead in the house, and on the Pretence of getting some money wherewith to defray the cost of burial, he went out and did not return. The Union paid the funeral charges, and had granted the wife outdoor relief. The cost incurred up to the present time was £1 us 6d. The prisoner, who is employed at the Liver Alkali Works, promised to pay the amount, and the costs, 8s 6d, and he was therefore discharged. WHITSUNTIDE HOLIDAYS AT RUNCORN.—Whit Tuesday was observed as a holiday in Runcorn by both tradespeople and worningmen. Steamers were run to Liverpool by the morning's tide, and conveyed 2,000 excursionists. About 1,500 persons also travelled to that city by train, the Ex- hibition no doubt being the centre of attraction. Frod- sham had attractions for 600, and there were 120 booked to Chester, and 600 to various places. There was also a trip to Llangollen arranged by the Camden Mutual Improve- ment Society, and upwards of 100 members and friends travelled by it. A very enjoyable day was spent amid , the beautiful scenery. The arrangements were carried I out lay Mr. H. Randle (president),:and Mr. J. T. Nickson I (secretary). SHOCKING RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT DITTON.—A shocking accident occurred on the London and Norta-Western Rail- way, at Ditton Junction, on Tuesday morning. John Man- non, a young man who lived at 26, Water-street, Widnes, was walking along the line from Widnes to Ditton, when he beard the 10-25 train from Manchester approaching behind. He stepped out of its way, but unfortunately into the path of the 10-28 train from Crewe, and he was knocked down and dangerously wounded. He had a severe scalp wound, his jaw was injured and his right thumb taken off, besides suffering from concussion of the brain. At the sug- gestion of Mr. Smith, the station master at Ditton, the un- fortunate man was conveyed in the same train to Liverpool, where his wounds were attended to at the Royal Infirmary.; Small hopes are entertained of his recovery. A LIVELY FRACAS AT DITTON. john Murphy, ft labourer, appeared at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, to answer a charge of assaulting Sarah Conroy. Mrs. Con- roy keeps a shop at Ditton, and takes in lodgers. It was alleged that on the night of the 9th inst. the defendant entered the house "rather drunk," and ordered his supper. The repast provided, however, did not please him. and "he cursed and went on something horrible." He was so quarrelsome that the services of Sergeant Coutts were re- quisitioned to put him out. Next day, when be went for his clothes, he assaulted his landlady, who received several blows on the face, and suffered from two black eyes.—The defendant expressed sorrow for having assaulted the woman, but said he did so under great prevocetion. The complain- ant and her daughter threw his clothes into the hack yard, and the daughter also threw a dish at him. He became enraged and rushed into the house, where there were sticks, pokers and plates flying at him.—The defendant was fined 2s 6d and costs 7s 6d. ROBBING A MoTHER.—At Widnes Petty Sessions. on Thursday, Julia O'Brien, was charged with having, on Fri- day the 11th inst., stolen a Bible, a shirt, and an apron, worth £1 13s, from the dwelling-house 15, Caroline-street. —Ann Furlong, a widow, said the prisoner was her daugh- ter, but did not live with her. She missed the articles from the house on the evening of the 10th inst. The shirt be- longed to a lodger, and Joseph Reading, assistant to Mr. Syred, pawnbroker, Waterloo-road, deposed to the prisoner attempting to pledge the articles.—Superintendent Barker said the prisoner was a very bad character, and had been convicted eleven times for drunkenness and felony. When she wanted money with which to procure drink she went to her mother's house aeid stole anything she could lay her hands on. He aska the Bench to deal severely with her. —The prisoner was sentgaced to three months' hard labour. Immediately on hearinPthe decision the prisoner, with a cry of rage, aimed what appeared to be a large stone at her mother, the missile narrowly escaping striking her head. It proved afterwards to be a prison bun. She was at once taken below.

THE NEW CHAIRMAN OF RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMIS- sToNERs.--Mr. P. Speakman, who was on Wedrresday elec- ted as chairman of the Board of Improvement Commis- sioners, has been a member of the Board for upwards of 13 yeps. He has previously ncupied the position of chair- man of the Highway and Sanitary Committee, which com- prised the whole Board, and during his entire public career has laboured untiringly in the interests of the community. In conjunction with the late Mr. Thomas Norman, Mr. Speakman took an active part in the movement which re- sulted in a reduction of the railway fares between Runcorn and Liverpool, of which the public now reap the advantage. To a great extent it was owing to the efforts of Mr. Speak- man that the approach to the bridge was improved by the construction of a slope, while he rendered valuable service in the negotiations that secured for the town the agree- ment with the Liverpool Corporation whereby that body is compelled to supply Runcorn with water from the Vyrnwy scheme, should there be a failure in local resources. Rc- cently he took a prominent part in the settlement of clauses with the promoters of the Manchester Shin Canal for the protection of the interests of the port. His selection as chairman of the local administrative authority is the reward of long and meritorious service.

WiIiTgrSITIDE AT WIDNAS —Havino. no attractions pro- vided in their own smoky town, the Widnesians went afar for their pleasures on Whit-Monday. The miserably wet wea- ther debarred them from a visit to the rural scenes of Hale, Lymtn, Frodshatn, and Helsby, which are in the immediate neighbourhood. The trip arranged by the Farnworth Parish Church authorities, however, conveyed about 600 persons to Lancaster and Morecambe, while about the same numl,er journeyed to that charming Welsh watering place, Llandudno, by the Rainford Mutual Improvement Society's trip. People went in their hundreds to Southport by the Cheshire Lines R tilwav, and on both lines the passengers to Liverpool and Belle \rue could be counted by the thou- sand. The Good Templars' trip to Sonthport was patron- ised by 600 persons. Runcorn was the destination of be- tween 2,000 and 3,000 people. As usual the sands near the promenade was the resort of the juvenile population,swings, "Aunt Sallies," and shooting galleries being located there. The town with the tradesmen's establishments closed had the appearance of a Sunday. There were, however, numer- ous worshipper of Bacchns, whose reeling gait, and noisy tones, were viewed with a lenient eye by the police authori- ties, who " kept the peace without the necessity of restor- ing to the "lockups" except in two instances.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The annual meeting of this Board was held on Wednesday morning, at the Town Hall, Waterloo-roo.d. There were present Messrs. P. Speakman, W. Fisher, Dobson, Taylor, Farrell, and Marshall (secretary). Mr. Marshall took the chair, and intimated that the only business was the election of a chairman for the ensuing twelre months. Mr. Dobson said be had great pleasure in moving that Mr. P. Speakman be appointed chairman for the ensuing year. He thought tlie ability and talent he had displayed during the short time he had occupied the position was a sufficient guarante that in future Mr. Speakman would maintain the honour and dignity of the chair during his term of office.

Mr. Fisher had much pleasure in seconding the proposi- tion. Mr. Speakman up to the present had been everything they could desire as a president over the Board's proceed- ings, and he thought they would only be doing their duty both to him and the ratepayers by appointing him chairman for the ensuing year. He would be the right man in the right place. The motion was cirried unanimously. Mr.Speakman then took the chair, and said it gave him great pleasure to accept the office of chairamn of the Com- missioners for the ensaing 12 months. He was obliged to the proposer of the resolution for the perhaps too flittering terms in which be had spoken of him, and also to Mr. Fisher, who seconded it. As he had said on a previous oc- casion, there was a dignity which belonged to the chair, and he trusted that each member would keep that dignity in- tact in the the interests of the unity and prosperity of the town. He thanked them very much for the honour they had conferred upon him that morning, and he could assure them that if he had their help during the ensuing 12 months as he had during the last three months nothing should be wanting on his part to conduct the affairs of the Board suc- cessfully.

div.head: whir MONDAY AT RUNCORN.
div.p: whir MONDAY AT RUNCORN.

Whit Monday is a festival celebrated in Runcorn with much display and not a little animated merrymaking. Al! classes make holiday from the highest to the lowest in the social scale, and to the normal populatien is added tlqou- sands of visitors from the surrounding villages. Flags float from numerous buildings, bands of music followed by the members of friendly societies and Sunday school scholars, attired in bright colours and bearing plc- banners, parade the streets, and lastly there are the attractions of a "folly fair." With a bright sun and a g,nial atmosphere the scene is a pretty one. But on the present occasion the display was without its usual effectiveness, and the enjoy- ment was almost wholly wanting. Rain descended without intermission from an early hour in the morning until noon, when there was a brief respite. A dull leaden sky, and a cold wind, however, gave no promise of amendment, and at one o'clock rain fell in torrents and continued all the afternoon. Under these circumstances the visitors were not SO numerous as in former years; but the Own was by no means deserted. Whilst only about 300 passengers depar- ted by train, the arrivals at the station numbered at least a thousand. This number included 200 from Liverpool, and the remainder came from Frodsham, Northwich, Winsford, land Chester. Upwards of a thousand persons came down the river Weaver by excursion steamers. But Widnes was tho largest contributor to the crowd. No less than between two and three thousand crossed the bridge from the chemi- cal centre in preference to seeking pleasures afar. Despite the unfavocable atmospheric conditions, the
WARRINGTON ELECTION.

The election campaign in Warrington may be said • to be now in full swing,both sides being actively pre- paring for the conflict. The address of Mr. John Cros- field, which will be found in another column, was placarded in the town early on Tuesday—before, in fact, the Conservatives had selected their candidate. The Tories, holwever, met on Tuesday evening, and decided, as was expected, that the sitting member, Sir Gilbert Greenall, should be brought forward lagain as their candidate. On the next day, Sir Gil- , bert's address was posted upon the wall; and each I candidate has sent his address and a card soliciting the vote and interest of every elector in the town.. The Liberals having got the start have so far kept it, being already far in advance in their canvass, which is proving all that could be desired. There are very few of the Liberal electors who are disposed 1 to abstain from voting because of their not being satisfied with the Government Home Rule Bill They recognise, after what has transpired with regard to Lord Carnarvon and Mr. Parnell, that Home Rule will be granted to Ireland in one form lor another, and they can better trust Mr. Gladstone than Lord Salisbury. As might be expected, the Irish electors are showing themselves enthusiastic in their support of Mr. John Crosfield, the Liberal candidate, who is pledged to support the Home Rule policy of the Prime Min- ister. They are offering their services in every ward, and. are anxious to render all the assistance they can. The English Catholics, too, thus far show themselves to be conscious of the mistake which some of them made at the last election, and have intimated that their vote will not on this occasion be given to the Conservative candidate. The fol- lowing letter from Father Scannell will be read with special interest and will no doubt have weight with the Irish and Catholic electors :

Lee House, June 17, 1886. DEAR Mn. ROBERTS,—I shall have much pleasure in recording my vote in favour of Mr. Crosfield at the coming elections. I have read his address with care, and I think it well deserving of the Catholic vote of Warrington—both English and Irish, and I hope it will be an enthusiastic and unanimous one. Wishing you every success, believe me to re- main, yours truly,

T. B. SCANNELL. The first meeting of the Liberal party will be held on Monday evening in Wycliffe Hail, and will be addressed by Mr. John Crosfield, Mr. McMinnies, Mr. William Crosfield, Mr. C. M. Percy, and other gentlemen. The electors will do well to be early in attendance in order to secure seats. Next Saturday it is intended to hold a mass meet- ing of working men in support of Mr. Gladstone 's Home Rule Bill in the Public Hall.

div.head: ELECTION CAMPAIGN.
div.p: THE ELECTION CAMPAIGN.

Speaking at Northampton on Friday afternoon, Lord Iddesleigh said reports from all parts of the kingdom showed that the Conservative cause never had brighter prospects than at present. Mr. Chamberlain indignantly repudiates an ' in- sinuation made on Thursday night at his own Divi- sional Council that he had used his influence against Mr. Broadhurst in Bordesley. The Carlisle Liberal Association, after passing a resolution disapproving of the sitting Unionist member, Mr. Ferguson's conduct, decided to ask Mr. Wilfrid Lawson, son of Sir Wilfrid, to stand as a Home Rule candidate.

The," Standard" -Understands that Her Majesty will arrive in London on Thursday next, and that the dissolution will take place on the following day. Writs for the election will not be issued before next Friday night at the earliest, and possibly not till Saturday, the 26th. The first nominations will pro- bably take place on Tuesday and Wednesday, and the result of the earliest borough elections will be known on Thursday, July Ist. Central News learns that, immediately after the division on the Home Rule Bill, Mr. Michael Davitt despatched the following cablegram to Mr. Egan, president of the Irish National League of Ametica The democracy will reverse the decision of Par- liament; counsel friends to have patience and con- fidence in the certain victory of the National cause. Cannot be defeated if the Irish people the world over keep down passion, and calmly and deter- minedly persevere in our present line." Mr. Gladstone, who was busily engaged on Friday morning, is delighted with his reception in Midlo- thian. To future arrangements there is nothing de- finitely settled except two meetings next week, one in Edinburgh on Monday afternoon, and one in Glas- gow on the following afternoon. Mr. Gladstone has, however, decided to speak at Manchester next week, but the day has not been fixed. Great pres- sure is being brought to bear on him to address a meeting at Dundee. In previous campaigns he has been asked to speak at that town, but has always found himself unable to do so. It is hoped now that he will consent.

The Central News says numerous inquiries have been made as to the formation of a fund to assist in defraying the strictly legal expenses at the forthcoming election of labour and other candid- ates, who are supporters of Mr. Gladstone's Irish policy. Generous promises of help have been made, and, as time presses, the following gentlemen have formed themselves into a committee for the pur- pose, and will be happy to hear from others who are willing to become associated with them :—Mr. Arthur J. Williams, .M.P., Professor Thorold Rogers, M.P,. Mr. P. Esselmont, M.P., Mr. Win. Phillips, Mr. E. H. Bayley, and Mr. Aubrey. Communica- tions may be addressed to Dr. Aubrey, National Liberal Club, Trafalgar-square, London.

div.head: WARRINGTON FARMERS' CLUB.
div.p: WARRINGTON FARMERS' CLUB.

A special general meeting of this club was held at the White Bull Inn, Ilorsemarket-street, on Wed- nesday evening, when Mr. John Marsh ,(Grappen- hall), presided, and there was a good attendance of members from various agricultural districts of Lan- cashire and Cheshire. • RAILWAY RATES. A letter was rec?ived from the- Loadon and North-Western Reilway Company in reard to the rates for the carriage of milk. After full consideration,. the lAter said, they did not see their way to make any alter- ation. As, however, the representations of the deputation to which the letter from the Farmers' Club referred, were unar consideration, the district of the club would be con- sidered at tha same time. The Cheshire Lines Railway Committee wrote saying that the communication of the club in regard to milk and farm produce rates would have atten- tion.

THE FLOODING or THE MERSEY.—The Bridgewater Navi- gation Company, in reply to a letter complaining of the flooding of the banks of the Mersey, and the consequent damage to land adjoining, caused by the erection of weirs, wrote saying that the club could not take any steps foe the mitigation of the floods, although they had lost no oppor- tunity of doing all they conveniently could in that direc- tion, and had already done much to relieve land which had from time immemorial been subject to floods. Any respon- sibility as to damage was repudiated by the company.—A short discussion followed the reading of the letter, but no resolution was passed on the subject. TIIE DISTRIBUTION OF FARM PRODUCE.—Mr. Percival, of Aston, read a paper on the "Distribution of Farm Pro• duce," submitting a scheme of distribution by means of co- operation. Prices had, he said, notwithstanding that more energy and economy had been exercised, fallen 30 percent.. and besides loss of profits, it now required twice as much time and expense to get their goods turned into cash. Agri- cultural produce formerly paid for storing during the winter months, but, owing to foreign competition, storing often now occasioned great loss. He thought that farmers should combine, and unitedly try to sell directly to the consumers of thickly populated towns, either by uniting themselves to co-operative societies, which he thought possible, or starting a co-operative society of tenants and landlords. He stig- gested the establishment of central stores, to be supplied direct with farmers' produce, and to be in telephonic or telegraphic communication with district stations, the tran- sit of heavy goods to be effected by traction engines and waggons. By this scheme, Mr. Percival surmised, the cost of transfer, market and retailers' expenses,would be.lessened, and farmers would benefit about 50 per cent. profit, without the produce being made dearer to the purchaser. If they progressed in a snail way, and had confidence in their busi- nets capacities, they might then offetethemselves as a united class to be incorporated with the wealthy and well organ- ised Co-operative Union of Manchester and district.—A. discussion followed the reading of the paper, after which the writer was thanked by a resolution, which was heartily carried.

WARRINGTON HIGHWAY BOARD.—A meeting of this Board was held at the Surveyor's office, Sankey- street, Warrington, on Wednesday, afternoon. Mr. R. Houghton (chairman) presided, and there were also present Captain Withington and Mr. W. F. Gooch (ex-officios),. Messrs. W. Royston, E. Marsh, G. Lawton, S. Bent, James Houghton, and J. Grounds. The Surveyor reported two or three en- croachments which had been made on the roads, and he was instructed to give the persons who had made them notice to remove the obstruction. He also reported that the County Surveyor had in- spected the main roads on the sth inst., and expressed himself well satisfied with their condi- tion. It was stated that the balance in the treas- urer's hand amounted to £385 13s. Bd.—There was nothing further of public interest before the Board,

THE CANDIDATES FOR NEWTON
DIVISION.

Since the announcement of the dissolution of Par- liament speculation has been rife throughout the Newton Division as to the probable candidates for the suffrages of the electors at the ensuing, general election. The gallant fight made last November and December by Colonel George McCorquodale, J.P., of the Willows, and the comparatively small majority secured by his opponent— a Tory Cabinet Minister, and acknowledged to be the strongest can- didate the Tories could put in the field—raised hopes among his many friends and admirers that he might again be induced to contest the constitu- ency, and on this occasion every circumstance seemed to favour the expectations of his suppor- ters that he would succeed in being placed at the head of the poll by a "thumping majority." But for a few weeks past it has been known that Col. McCorquodale would not again come forward as a candidate, and with regret tile Liberal leaders of the Division were obliged to look in other directions. The Executive of the Liberal Association of the Newton Division delegated the selection of certain gentlemen for submission as candidates to the Liberal "300," to two members of the Executive. Several steps have since been taken in the matter, but up to Wednesday night, in the present week, nothing definite in regard to a Liberal candidate had been decided upon. Several paragraphs have been published regarding the matter, but they were entirely unauthorised and inaccurate. The Consep- vs.tives have lately been very active in preparing for the election. No other name beyond that of the present member, Sir Richard Assheton Cross, is mentioned, and on every hand it is taken for granted that he will again come forward in the Conservative interest.

A meeting of the Newton-le-Willows eection of the Liberal "300" of the Newton Division, was held in Newton Town Hall, on Wednesday even- ing, and there was a full representative attendanee, including delegates from Park-side and Golborne Dale. Mr. W. Urquhart (chairman) presided. The chairman and Mr. Rawlinson, the Newton represen- tatives on the Executive Council, reported at some length on the steps taken up to that period with the view of bringing a Liberal candidate before the constituency, and a lengthy discussion ensued. A unanimous feeling was expressed that there should be a contest, and arrangements were made therefor. A hearty interest and anxiety to work for the succe,ss of the Liberal candidate was manifested.

div.head: LIBERAL CANDIDATE.
div.p: THE LIBERAL CANDIDATE.

A specially summoned meeting of the Executive of the Newton Liberal Association was held in one of the rooms of the Earlestown and. District Club on Thursday evening. The business was stated to be of an important character, and there was a large attendance. The chair was occupied by Mr. G. W. Rawlins, of Rainhill. After some consideration, it was unanimously resolved to submit the name of Sir George Errington as the Liberal candidate for adoption by the Liberal Council of 300. Sir George Errington is the eldest son of the late M. Errington, Esq., of Cassino, Dublin County, and was born in 1839. In the course of his education, he went successively to Ushaw College and Durham and Dublin Universities. He. is a justice of the peace for Tipperary, Knight of Justice of the order of Malta, and was created a baronet of England in 1885. He sat for Longford Co. as member of Parlia- ment from 1874 to 1885. .He is a Liberal Roman Catholic who is held in the highest esteem by his co-religionists; and it is believed that unofficially, through his influence with the Vatican, he was of great service in helping to pre- serve a good feeling towards the English Govern- ment during the trying and troublous times that have been witnessed in Ireland during the past few years. He has deserved well of the Liberal party, and it is to be hoped that, if he is adopted as the candidate by "the 300," as we believe he will, he will receive the united and enthusiastic support of all sections of the Liberal party in the Newton Division. .

It may be added that Sir George is trustee of the will of the late Marchioness Stapleton-Bretherton, of The Hall, Rainford, who left large estates in Rainford, Ditton, Cronton, Widnes, and the neigh- bourhood of Wigan, leaving Sir George a consider- able estate at Lackham, in Wiltshire. The first husband of the Marchioness was William Gerard, Esq., brother to the present Lord Gerard. The pro- posed Liberal candidate is on his way at the present moment from America.

On April 11th, 1886; a reporter of the "New York Sun" gave an account of an interview. with Sir George Errington. His mission to Rome was the first subject spoken of, and that led up to the Irish question. Sir George refutes the idea that he had used his influence at Rome to prejudice the Pope against Ireland, and induce him to condemn and oppose the National movement. "I have always been and am still," he said, "most strongly in favour of Home Rule, even in its widest inter- pretations, and any opinions expressed by me at Rome or elsewhere were' never directed against Home Rule as such, but simply against the ex- cesses which unfortunately discredited the agitation. I have never said a word against a political and constitutional movement in itself, which I regarded as perfectly legitimate." The concluding part of the interview is taken up with a eulog,ium on Mr. Parnell, of whom Sir George Errington apparently entertains a high opinion, a4nd a reference to the American sympathy with the Irish.
SELECTION OF CONSERTATIVE CANDIDATE FOR WARRINGTON.

On Tuesday,evening the council of the Warring- ton Conservative Association met in the Assembly- room, at the Conservative Club, Sankey-street, to consider the selection of a Conservative candidate for the borough at the next election. Captain Rey- nolds presided, and amongst• those present were Major Litton, the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, Messrs. W. Beamont, R. Davies, J. Davies, S. M. Webster, J. Pierpoint, R. Pierpoint, R. W. Francomb, Mackie, W. J. Burgess, J. Fairclough, H. Greenall, T. Sut- ton, Wm. Sharp, T. Jolley, T. Cawley, J. Roberts, J. Taylor, J. C. Whittle, G. Y. Bolton, J. Collin, W. ' Bolton, R. W. Marsh, W. D. Jeans, D. Jones, R. Smith, A. Woods, T. Hutchinson, R Isherwood, J. Hampson (agent), and T. 0. Speakman. Letters of apology for non-attendance were read from the Hon. Leopold Powys, and Messrs. J. White, H. Haynes, J. Tinsley, Bleckly, W. Carson, C. J. Nichol- son, P. Naylor, and others. Mr. Bleckly wrote that on this occasion they could have no difficulty in selecting a candidate if the one who carried their colours so triumphantly at the last election' would take charge of them again. Under present circum- stances it was of vital importance that they should have a candidate who could win. "Sir Gilbert," he wrote, "has proved that he can do this against the best Crosfield they could bring. He will not lower his colours to a weaker one." Mr. John White inti- mated that he should do his best to increase the Con- servative majority from 776 to 1,776 and Mr. James Tinsley, in a brief epistle, supposed that the Conser- vatives would all be united in the selection of "the grand old man "for their candidate. He added that he did not mean the "G. 0. M. of Hawarden," but the "Grand Old Man" of Walton Hall, who was always ready to help forward every good work in the town, and of whose generosity they had had so recently another example. The CHAIRMAN, in mentioning the object of the meeting, said that Sir Gilbert Greenall had unreservedly placed him- self in the hinds of his party, and was willing to fall in with whatever they said or did. From his knowledge of the elections and their feelings he thought Sir Gilbert was the etrongeet man they could bring forward. No one could contradict the assertion that Sir Gilbert was advanced in years, but they could say of him that they had never known a man who bore his age so lightly. There was no one whom he knew who seemed to naves carried out his politi- cal duties in an easier way than he (Sir Gilbert) had done. He advised them to select as candidate their old and tried friend. (Applause). Mr. W. BEAMONT endorsed what the chairman had re- marked, and seid he believed they conld not find a man who had been more true to his trust than Sir Gilbert Greenall had been. He had no hesitition in proposing that Sir Gil- bert Greenall be selected as the candidate. Mr. Beamont condemned the policy of Mr. Gladstone, and iu conclusion urged the Conservatives to be united. They were, he said, entitled to have the support of the Liberals. He was as Liberal as any one, though not a Liberal in 'name, and he would have no abuse continued. Many Liberals boasted about being Liberal who were nothing but illiberal in principle. (Cheers.) Mr. JOHN ROBERTS seconded the resolution, and, on be- half of the working-men of the borough, alleged that he bad on many occasions had the opportunity of ascertaining that they considered that Sir Giibert Greenall was the right man to be put forward as the candidate. (Applause.) They would feel convinced in fighting for Sir Gilbert that they were fightioo for a very honourable and straightforward gentleman, and for one who had always done his duty, had rallied round them in every shape and form; and if they fought for him in that spirit he was sure they would, as at the last election, secure a victory. (Applause.) Mr. BautaineETr supported the proposition. The issues at the forthcoming election were, be said, important, and what the electors had to do was to return their candidate to uphold the integrity of the empire. (Applause.) Mr. ROBERT PIERPOINT said that it must not be thought that because they won at the list election it was an abso- lute certainty that they would win at the next, and urged them to leave nothing undone, lest by some mistake a single vote should be lost. Since the last election, Mr. Gladstone had seen the necessity for giving to the Irish what he called Home Rule; but he (Mr. Pierpoint) asked those present not to be deceived lity names. (Hear, hear.) He did net like such useless Greek words as autonomy.. (Laughter.) Let them not be deceived by the name of Home Rule, for it really meant the repeal of the Uoion. "(Hear, hear.) He hoped they would show by their voice that the Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland as it was now should for ever be indivisible. (Applause.) Mr. ROBERT DAVIES, who also spoke in favour of the re- solution, remarked that they must at once admit that the umbrella, the old Gladstone gingham, was at last so shrunk 1 up that it would not cover the Liberal 'party. (Laughter.) They found the National Liberal Federation turning out Mr. 1 Chamberlain; Mr. Chamberlain's lieutenant, Mr. Schnad- horst, waxing fat and kicking, and actually going to com- mence business on his own amount; and they found the candidate for Warrington ha l at last broken ties with his guide, philosopher, and friend, Mr. John Bright. (Laugh- ter.) Was it any wonder, if such dissensions arose, that there should be differences between the North and South of Ireland when one of the roost important measures that had ever come before him as an elector was presented to them for determination at the coming election? (Applause.) Mr. Gladstone had brought in a bill—an apple of discord_ which had separated North and South Ireland, which was separating his own party, and involving what was not long ago a united Ljberal party in one common ruin. He hoped Warrington would return their trusty, worthy, and old re- presentative. He had read the address of the new candidate that day, and the idea conveyed to his mind was that his friend Mr. Crosfislcl was possessed of more imagination than toe had given him credit for. (Laughter.) They would be good friends with Mr. John Crosfield. They would fight him fairly; but what they would like him to do would be to give him time to perfect to the enoet perfect pitch of absolute perfect "perfection" that article of domestic manufacture which they saw advertised on the walls. (Laughter.) If he would only attend to that business they would be good neighbours, mad stay at home to shop. They would leave "Dry Soap ;" they would not look upon "Sun- light Soap" or "Magic Soap," but leaving all others they would cleave to the " Perfeclon Soap." (Laughter) They would do anything for him except part with their present propositionl member. r.ll'. THE EXAM' NE R , SATURDAY. JUNE 19, 1886. _.• Mr. Gladstone. (Hear, hear.) He supported the re so *ion. The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON said it seemed to him there could be no doubt that they would at the next elec- tion lose the Irish vote, and to counterbalance that they should get the help of the Liberals who would not join in the process by which the Empire in which.they lived would be split•up.into a number of independent states. They had the influence in that direction of Mr. Peter Rvlands, whose independent action he admired, of men like Mr. Bright and Mr. Chamberlain, and ef Mr. Spurgeon for the Noncon- formists, for whom he (Mr. Carleton) had the greatest rPspect. • Mr. THOMAS JOLLEY having also spoken in favour of the resolution, it was put to the meeting and carried, and Sir Gilbert Greenall, having been requested to enter the room, was informed by the Chairman of the decision of the meet- ing:. _

-Sir GILBERT GRRENALL, M.P., in reply, said that any- thing more kind or more flattering than their feeling to- wards him it was impossible to conceive. (Applause.) It was but a short time since they met to consider political subjects, and be was sure they did not expect, and could not have dreamt of being called together again for iaolitical objects so soon or so immediately. (Hear, hear.) They had then at the head of the Government, with which they did not then agree, and with which Government they were still less in agreement at the present moment, a Prime Minister boasting of his political strength and of his Par- liamentary numbers. Where was that special political strength? Where were the boasted numbers gone They had disappeared entirely, and the big majority had fallen Into a minority of 30, and the majority, in his judgment, did express, and express clearly, the opinions of the elec- tors. (Cheers.) He would not, with their permission, dwell any longer on political matters. A question had been put to him, and he was bound and ready to answer it. (Hear, hear.) He was one of them, he belonged to them, for they had made him politically vrat he was. (Applause.) Never for one moment had he doubted their loyalty and fealty to him, and nevec for one moment had he ceased to regard them with respect and affection. (Applause.) They had not left him for one moment, and he could not, after the kind feelings which had been shown to him that evening, say that he either could or would leave them. (Cheers.) If they accepted him, and took him as their candidate, he was prepared and willing to stand—(loud applause)—and on his part he would not be found wanting where he had either time or ability to act for them. There were two im- possibilities he found at that moment—two great impos- sibilities. The first was that they should ever sever them- selves from him, and the second impossibility was—and it was an impossibility—that he akould ever separate himself from them. (Cheers.) From that moment, and with a definite and fixed object in view, they were one—(hear, hear)—they would go together, they would work together, and they would rejoice together in their success. (Loud applause.) They bad entered upon an engagement, and if they want forth manfully with the intention to conquer, using the means true soldiers always used, they would sue- ceed. (Hear, hear.) But let there be no halting, let every soldier, let every man, every elector, consider that the bat- tle rested with him. (Hear, hear.) He was very grateful to them. He was with them, and they would go forth to- gether, and would rejoice victoriously together. (Loud ap- plause.) • The meeting then concluded with a vote of thanks to the , Chairman.

EARLESTOWN. Gocrn TEMPLARY.—On Wednesday Brother James Bird, of St. Helens, V.S.J.T., visited the Pride of Rules- town Lodge of Juvenile Templar., and delivered an in- teresting address on juvenile temperance work. . THE NEW COLLIERY AT GOLBORWB.—The new colliery which is being sunk by Messrs. R. Evans and, Co., in con- nection with their plant at Gelborne, is making satisfactory progress, and has already proved a boon to not a few fami- lies whose principal supporters bad been out of work for a considerable time. The sinking operations are continued day and nigbt, the men working what is known as three shifts of eight hours each. &nom AT Isizwrow TOWN FrALL.—A somewhat un- usual scene was witnessed at the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday, when Mary McLoughlin was charged with being drunk and disorderly at Golf-pane on the 6th inst.—After two constables had given evidence, the defendant strongly denied the charges, and excitedly accaused the officers of be- ing "drunken, nasty rascals.”— She was then cautioned by the Magistrates' Clerk, who said if she was not quiet she would have to be locked up. The defendant continued to Incoherently express her opinions, and the Bench inflicted a fine of 5s and costs, and ordered her to be removed from the court. •

STREET OBSTREMION. —B Of ore Messrs. R. Houghton, C. Pilkington, and W. F. Gooch, at the Newton Town Hall on Saturday, John Byrne, of Manchester, was sum- moned for obstructing the street at Earlestown, on the let inst. P.C. Hunt stated that on Race Tuesday he saw the defendant obstructing Railway-street, Earlestown, by draw- ing a horse and deg cirt across it. He was fined 58 and costs.—Edward Fletcher,. employed by Mr. Dixon, cab and coach proprietor, St. Helens and Earlestown, was summoned for obstructing Legh-street„ Earlestown, with twe horses and a waggonette, on Pridav night, the 4th inst. P.C.'s Lloyd and Lee gave evidence that defendant was engaged conveying passengers to and from Haydock, and he drew out into the street, which was obitructed for three or four minutes. A fine of 25 fld and costs was imposed.—Joseph Lawrenson, driver of a spring cart, was also summoned for a similar offence committed on the same date, and was fined 2s 64 and cots.

FOOTBALL. - Thomas McGrail and Patrick McGrail, young men, wire summoned at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, for playing at football with an elastic ball in Heath-street, on the afternoon of Sunday,3oth May. They were each fined 2s Gd and costs.

A. MIDNIGHT DISTURBANCE.—At the Newton Petty Ses- sions, on Saturday, John Battersby, Peter Anderton, John Anderton, James St;rrup, Rebecca Battersby, and Elizabeth Anderton were summoned for committing a breach of the peace at Go!borne on the midnight of Saturday, 15th May. The defendants were quarrelling and using btd lan- guage, and many persons who had gone to bed in the neighbourhood were disturbed. Each of the defendants was ordered to ha bound over to keep the peace.

div.head: HAYDOCK.
div.p: HAYDOCK.

HAYDOCIC READING AND DBBATING SOCIETY.—The first monthly meeting for the summer season in connection with the Haydock Reading and Debating Society was held on Thursday night in the Reading Room. About fifty mem- bers attended, and Mr. James Bailey presided. Mr. R. M. Prescott gave his report as delegate to the Manchester Working-men's Clubs Association, which was adopted and acknowledged with a cordial vote.of thanks to Mr. Prescott, on the motion of Mr. Johnson, seconded by Mr. E. Jackson. Several subjects were afterwards suggested as suitable for impromptu speaking, and the ballot resulted in the ques- tion The Employers' Liability Act" being brought for- ward. The order of speaking was also balloted for, and the introduction of the subject fell to the chairman, who was followed by Messrs. R. M. Prescott, J. C. Westworth, John- son, Taylor, Newton (Earlestown), Andrews, Arnold, &c. Several creditable speeches of an intelligent character were given upon the topic, and the first venture of the kind was considered very satisfactory. A HAYDOCK MAN ROBBED AT ST. HELENS. —At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Monday, John Forster, a young man residing in 5 Court, Crab-street, was charged with stealing 2s GLI from the person of Charles Forshaw, on Sat- urday night. Prooecutor said he was standing in College. Street, where a man was selling goats. He wanted to buy a goat, and he gave the man in charge 2s f3d for one, but the man gave the tireney back to him and would not sell the goat. While the money was in his hand the prisoner struck his hand, and the money fell to the ground. Prisoner picked the money up ; witness asked him for it several times, but he refused to give it to him.—P.C. Cruildert de- posed te apprehending the accused who, in reply to the charge, said "I am charged with something that I am not guilty of."—Prisoner denied that be either knocked the half-crown out of the proecutor's band of picked it up, and he called John Qornall as a witness, who said the man sel- ling the goats knocked the money out of prosecutor's hand, and it fell among straw.—Prisoner was fined 103 and costa, or seven days' imprisonment.

EXCURSTON.—On Whit-Monday the Young Men's Bible Class in connection with Zion Sunday Schools had their an- nual trip, this time to Southport. They were acc3mp4nied by Mr. Thomas Yates, teacher, and other friends. An en- joyable day was spent in spite of the downpour of rain. FATAL ACCIDENT AT CARR COLLIERY, WHISTON.—On Friday, a middle-aged man named Charles Roberts, em- ployed at the above colliery and residing at Prescot, was injured in his spine by a fall of coal, and died the next day, leaving a widow and fiva children to mourn their loss. An inquest was held at the Eagle and Child Inn, Pres: cot, on Monday, and a verdict of accidental death was re- turned.

CAUTION TO DRIVERS.—At the Present Petty Sessions, on Tuesday. before Mr. W. L. Evans and Mr. J. C. Gamble, Joseph Norris, Kirby, was summoned for riding on the shaft of a waggon drawn by four horses, without reins at Knowsley on the 4th inst. He was fined 2s 6d and cats. —James Robinson, carter, Kirby, was fined a like amount for being over one hundred yards from his horse and cart, over which he bad not proper control, at Knowsley, on the 4th inst.—Andrew Gormln, carter, Roby, summoned for leaving his horse and waggon on the highway, without anyone in charge, at Roby, on the 3rd just, was fined 2s Gil and costs

PITCH AND Toss—At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Joseph Woodward,-eollief, Prescot, Henry Abra- ham, collier, Prescot, Henry Pitchford, ironworker, Huyton, Samuel Parker, ironworker, Huyton, and William Jones,, ironworker, Huyton, were summoned for playing at pitch and toss. The defendants Woodward, Pitchford, and Jones- appeared. When the case was called Superiutendent Barker said the officer in the case was unable to appear, and he would withdraw the summonses agginst the three defrndants present if they would nay the cost 4F This the defendants promised to do. The case against the other defendants was adjourned.

&Hoeg. TREAT.—On Wednesday last the Sunday school in connection with the Church of England had their annual treat in Knowsley Park, kindly lent by the Earl of Derby. From 7GO to 800 children assembled and marched through the town, headed be the Whiston brass band, conductor, Mr. J. Corm. The banner was carried bearing the date nu, Prescot Church Sunday Schools, and the Rev. H. A. Mc- Naghten and Rev. F. R. Lee, teachers, and other ladies and gentlemen were present. Tea was served in the assembly rooms, kindly lent by Mr. W. L. Evans. Afterwards the children returned to Know, ley Park for the remainder of the evening for games, die. The afternoon being fine, brought a large number of visitors to the park. SINGULAR APPEAL CASES.—At the .Prescot Petty Ses- sions on Tuesday, before Messrs. W. L. Evans and J.. C. Gamble, Mr. S. H. Hartley, clerk to the Assessment Com- mittee, made a singular application. He said he had been instructed to appear against the appellants in appeal cases by the vicar of Prescot, the vicar of Sutton, and the Pro- testant scholars of the King's College, Cambridge. The three defendants named had appealed against rates in twelve of the parishes comprising the Prescot Union, for the rating of small tithes and rent tithea. The Assees- ment Committee, having beard objections against the rating of that particular class of property, gave to the objectors such redress as they thought sufficient. The appellants gave notice of appeal to tbat sessions, as the magistrates were required to fix four seesions in each year for hearing' appeals. The Assessment Committee, on receiving notice of the appeals, prepared for that sessions, and on Monday last, a little before 12 o'clock, received through him (Mr. Hartley) notice of the abandonment of the appeals. In the meantime the cases bad been prepared, and he had to ask the Bench, haying the same power as the court of Quarter Sessions, to grant to the Amsessment Committee and the Oyerseers of the townships affected, certificates of the con- firmation of the rates so appealed against. He was further to ask the Bench to allow °oats to the Assessment Commit- tee up to the time of the appeals having been abandoned by the three appellants.—Mr. Hartley was then sworn, and produced the notices of appeal signed by Frederick Smith for and on behalf of the appellants. He suggested that the sum of one guinea should be allowed for coats incurred in each of the twelve townships.—The Chairman : Are they aware that you are going to make the application P—Mr. Hartley said it had already been decided that notice need not be given to appellants on the abandonment of appeals I —After some further consideration, the magistrates decided to allow a sum of 14s 6d in each of the townships.

ALLIDGED SUNDAY DRINKING MP NEWTON At the the Newton Petty, Sessions on Saturday, William (irim- shaw and Lawrence Roach were summoned for being on the licensed premises of George Naylor,. the Swann Inn, New- ton Common, during prohibited bourn, on Sunday, 30th May. The defendant Roach cid not appear. P.C. Hunt stated that at five minutes past eleven o'clock on the fore- noon of the date named he Yisited the Swan Inn, and found the defendant there. The defendant Gritnsbaw pleaded guilty, and was fined 5s and costs; and a warrant was issued for the apprehension of Roach.. Superintendent Weir stated there was a summons against the landlord, but Mr. J. 0. Swift, who had been engaged to defend, had written. asking for an adjournment. The case was adjourned until the next sessions. MB ATHLETIC SPORTS AT ASHTON. The sports arranged to take place on the Recreation Ground, at Ash- ton, on Whit Monday, had to be postponed to to-day (Satur- day) on account of the rain, which fell heavily nearly the whole of the afternoon. Beyond a few heats of one of the principal races the only event proceeded with was the first round of the football contest, in which most of the local clubs had a team competing. The Earlestown club was represented by James Appleton, R. Green, J. Whalley, G. Clough, J. W. Sims, W. Rich, and T. Siddeley, and they won their tie by scoring three goals and five corner kicks to their oppo- nents (Worthington's team) nil. Havdock St. James and Golborne teams played a close match, but the latter eecured the victory by a minor point. Haydock Temperance also won their tie.

SPECIAL SERVICE. The services in the Congregational Church, Crow-lane. on Sunday, were closely associated with the sad proceedin, of the preceding day. It had been arranged that the Rn William Davies, of Woolton, should have preached s special funeral sermon, but, as was annouaced by the Ray. r3Enes Matt during the service on Saturday, that rev. gentleman. had been taken suddenly ill and was reluctantly MI pelted to give up the engagement. The pulpit was acne! ingly occupied in the morning by the pastorrthe Rev- '4:3: Ailatt, who touchingly alluded to the late Mr. Ashton. the congregation entered the church the organist (gr. Caldwell) rendered "Behold the Lamb of Clod," and at close of the service "I know that my Redeemer liveth was played. During the service the choir, conducted bY Mr. Dick, impressively sang the anthem, " Blessed are the dead.." The evening preacher was the Rev. F. N. Shilun'jtil (Primitive Methodist). The choir sang "As the Ilear —, panteth," and the organist rendered But Thou didst nee leave his soul," and the Hallelujah chorus" from Mount of Olives." The services on each occasion were we" attended.

ASHTON. the The death of Mr. Charles Ashton, last Week, under, „, sad circumstances reported in our last issue seems to en; created a genuine feeling of sorrow, which, it is exPecte a will be expressed in a tangible shape. A proposal tbattha memorial should be erected by public subscription aver Pi remains in the Crow-la Congregational Church yard b 39., been well received. After the funeral on Saturday afterne7e the workmen from the Viaduct Waggon Works met in t yard of the Viaduct Institute and held an open-air meetiehibe to consider thesubject. Mr. B. Harrison presided, and h was supported by F. Harwood (chief foreman) and t other foremen. Mr. Harrison briefly explained the °WI!, of the meeting, and in speaking of the late Mr. Ashton he had fallen out of their ranks and they would have erTs. cults, in replacing him. He had fallen out of their when he was so ?till of promise. They had all felt that was as it were, a flower in the bed, but before he had tirne!;" expand he was taken away from them. They all regretted and they believed it would be a graceful act to put a Inepti: moot over his head that will show his last resting PI a c`. He had to say that Mr. Harwood had kindly consented ,t,af head' the subscriotious with a guinea. (Hear, hear.) v,_ , course it was not expected that workmen would contrite largely, but if they would all contribute a little they woula be aye to put a handsome stone over his head, and ?all which would be worth looking upon. (Applause.)--i; John Gooding, after observing that he did not exP!'rti to have been called upon to saw anything W" that regard to the late Mr. Ashton, remarked they in the office were a little more int matAy connected with him than the general bedZ of woektnen, and he could to a great extent coincide viitm every tribute of praise of not only Mr. Harrison, but ale° in relation to whet they had heard at Crow-lane that after. noon. There were little things that came out at times • which really showed the true character of the man, eaPe; chilly among the workmen, much more so than some things. A few days before Mr. Ashton's death he (ir Geoding) heard one of the workmen say "If we go to Air,; • Ashton for anything we ale always sure of a civil answer- (Hear, hear.) His remarks would be but few, for as their had heard at Crow-lane, actions spoke louder than wordr,s; In his opinion if they follovred the hints thrown out, a each put his little together, he thought they could erect over Mr. Aehton's grave a tombstone, which would bea credit to them and show their respect for him and his family.—Mr. Harrison : Will anyone move a resolution on the subject ?—Mr. John Jones moved that subscriptions be collected for the purpose of erecting a memorial stone Over the grave of the late Mr. Ashton.—Mr. John Davi" seconded the resolution, which was passed unanimouslY,-- The proceedings then terminated.

WIIIT'rUNTIDE AT EARLESTOWN. • Though several of the principal shops in Earlestown were closed on Monday, all the works in the neighbourhood were. in fall swing, as usual, and consequeetly the holiday was not generally observed. As in other parts of the country. rain fell heavily in Earlestown and Newton almost through- out the entire day. Thd Viaduct Wagon Works of tin London and North-Western Railway Company cease business on Wedneerlay evening until Monday morning next. The Vulcan Foundry ,and the Newton Printing - Works have not been stopped during the week. The holidaYs commenced on Thursday, when the weather was beautifulll fine, and the field-treats to the children attending one or two Sunday schools were of a very successful character. WIT AND HUMOUR.

Friend in need—A poor relation. Goes without saying—The deaf and dumb alphabet. What is taken from you before you possess it ?—Your photograph. Why are cobblers eligible for medical diplomas ?—Because they are skilled in the art of heeling. "The pleasantest way to take cod-liver oil," says an old gourmand, "is to fatten pigeons with it, and then eat the pigeons." Some years ago an English member of Parliament, hearing Barmah mentiped, observed, "Oh, yes, Barmah ! I had a cousin who was out there for some time; but he always Called it Bermuda." A DARLING GOING TO COLLEGE.—First small boy: Say, Johnnie, where are you in Sunday school ?—Second small boy: Oh, we're in the middle of original sin.—First small boy: That ain't much; we're past redemption. The new coachman has been advised to be scrupulously polite to his employer if he wishes to keep his place. Ac- cordingly, when his master visits the stable, the following conversation takes place. "Well, John, how are the horses this merning ?" "Quite well, sir, thank you. Bow are you?" Incgtessn PARENTS.—A Justice of the Peace at Clayton, Ga., was awakened from his slumbers the other night to marry an eloping couple—Jephtha Littleton, aged 82, and Ruth Ann Thompson, aged 75. The parents of the elopers are much incensed, and it is feared will not forgive the giddy youngsters. Sandy: I want a cake o' soap, Mr. M'lntosh.—Chemist : I canna let ye has a cake o' soap on th' Sawbath day, Sandy.—Sandy : But ye sell'd that lassie peppermint-drops! —Chemist: Ay, ye can Book peppermints in the kirk, but ye canna wash yersel' there! HIIRROOSH!—An excited Irishman who was declaiming about justice to Ireland was asked by a London friend, "What is it really that you and your countrymen want ?" He replied, "We do not know what we want, sir; but, by the powers, we are determined to have it !" A. tnan-servant applied for an engagement. "Whore have you been employed ?" • "I lived with a dentist." "And why did you leave your master ?" "Oh, I couldn't stand it any longer! . All the people who came to see my master had such a melancholy air that it gave me the megrims !" ~ ADTANCED IN. CHRISTIANITY.-011 the Pacific Coast Chinamen who "profess and call themselves Christians" are given the preference as domestic servants, and for this reason it is suspected that many of them attend the Chinese missions and claim to be converted. One of these self- seeking converts recommended himself as a cook to a lady in Portland, On., by the proud announcement: "Me Clistian Chinaman; me can say, 'T'inkle, t'inkle 'ittle 'tar.'" Sheridan allowed his son to join a dinner party when he was quite young. The father was defining what wit was, when the boy interrupted him, saying he could give a better definition. "Well, what is it, Tom ?" "That which sparkles and cats," replied the son. "Then," observed Sheridan, "as you have sparkled, you can now cut!"—and poor Tom lost the remainder of his dinner. At an episcopal dinner party recently a layman was giving an account of a visit to the House of Commons, and, speak- ing of an old member, said, "But, poor old fellow, I couldn't understand a word he said. He might have been speaking Hebrew, or Greek, or Arabic, he is so toothless." One of the bishops at once interrupted with, " Ah, then I suppose he spoke gum-arabic !" A student said to a distinguished lawyer one day, "I can- not understand how circumstantial evidence can be stronger than positive testimony." " I will illustrate it," said the lawyer. "My milkman brings ine a can of milk, and says, 'Sir, I know that is pure milk, for I drew it from the cow, washed the can thoroughly, strained it into the can, and nobody else has handled it.' Now, when I take the cover from the can, out leaps a bull-frog. surely the frog is stronger evidence than the man!" THE DANGER OF A LITTLE LEARNING —Teacher: "Why, Freddie, how did you get those black and blue welts on your arm ?" Scholar: "Them'a your fault, teacher !" Teacher : "My fault? What do you mean ?" Scholar (sobbing reminiscently): "Why, you told me it was a poor rule that didn't work both ways. So, when I went home I took pa's new two-foot rule that doubles up on a hinge, and bent it back till it worked both ways; and then pa said I'd broken I the joints, and he went and got his razor strap. I think it was a mean trick to play on a feller, and I'll never forgive

you." TREASoN!—Overheard whilst watching the Australian cricket team at practice. Fair feminine athlete: "Splendid fellows, these! What physiques! What muscles! There's a hit for you! How charming! You'll have to pull your- selves together, Lord X, if you ara going to retain our hearts this season." "Oh, bear with our infirmities one summer more, Miss Z.; tax your constancy yet another season! Next year we are going to have over a team of Australian lady lawn-tennis players. Then you will be free to worship whom you list; we shill have idols of our own." WITT THE SIIN NEVER SETS On THE QUEEN'S DO3IINIONS. —The Transvaalers are generally offensively rude to Eng- lishmen; but, as a yule, their insults "lack point." There is however something almost like wit in the Boer's retort recorded by Mr. J. J. Aubertin in his Six Months in Cape Colony and Natal. "After a hot wrangle, • What is the use of a handful of rude animals like you,' said an English- man, pretending to beat the country like ours? Do you know that the sun never sets on the Queen's dominions?' What of that? asked the Transvaaler. Why, it shows our enormous power!' It rather shows something else in my opinion.' 'What may that be?' •It shows you are such a set of rascals that Providence can't trust you in the dark.'" Hs SUPPLIED THE Prtovrsroxs.—" Uncle Stead" is What they called a shrewd old gentleman who used to live in Winthorp, Me., a little way out of the village. One of his fellow-citizens was a man naard Lovejoy. " Uncle Stead" met Lovejoy in the villsgi one day, and he said to him, "Lovejoy, there's a poor oman living on the outskirts of the town who needs some provisions. I'm willing to supply her; but I've sold my horse, and have no means of getting the stuff to her. Now I'll buy her a barrel of flour and a ham and other supplies if you'll carry t' em out to her with your team." Lovejoy said he would be very glad to do it. Accordingly "Uncle Stead" bought a barrel of flour, a ham, a quantity of sugar, &c., and., telling Lovejoy where the woman lived, sent him off on his !grand of charity with the good things in his vehicle. Lovejoy easily found the house where the woman lived. Ile unloaded the goods, puffing like a grampus as he rolled the flour in, and said to the woman, "Mr. Stead sent you the provisions. He's a mighty kind-hearted man to send you all these things." "Well, I don't know why he shouldn't send them to, me," exclaimed the woman, in a surprised tone. " lies my husband !"

them—Advt. CYCLONE AT DEAL.—The town of Deal, which was about seven years ago visited by a most disastrous cyclone was on Monday again visited by a similar phenomenon. A large quantity of tiles were displaced where the wind caught the roofs of houses, anl on the beach many of the boats were lifted bodily from the ground by the wind and carried a considerable distance. Some of them were blown together two or three in a heap and much damaged by the force of the collision. The cyclone touched first the village of Sholden, near Deal, where it destroyed some vineries and nurseries. It caused great havoc to some farm builditgs at Middle Deal. Trayellibg eastward across the South- Eastern Reilway, the extraordinary force of the wind was manifested by its taking a heavy iron crane, used for un- loading. trucks, and twisting it round like a top. A tree was also uprooted and blown into another garden. The cyclone lasted not more than ten minutes, and terminated in the Downs, where it had a curious effect on the water, but for- tunately did not take any shipping in its scope. HOmE RULE DISTURBaNCESUS MANCHESTER.—SEvERAL INJURED —At Manchester City Police Court, on Monday, Martin Healer, Thomas Rowan, Patrick Finnigan, John Fagan, and Thomas Doherty were charged with riotous behaviour in Indigo-street, Ardwick, on Saturday night. The prisoners were middle-aged men of the labouring class. They appear to have met in the house of Doherty on Sat- urday night, and to have had there a quantity of drink. About half-past eleven they turned into the street armed with firearms and other weapons. and raised the cry "Three cheers for Home Rule and the Connaught lads." Without provocation, they attacked almost every passer-br, and in tthhereemyee/iareswobf age, iachthey created one of them struck a child which was in the arms of its 'nether, and seriously fractured its skull. A girl named Violet Hall also received a -cut over the left eye, and a man named Hines was stal,bed in the left arm. Several other persons were also injured, and great alarm was felt in the neigh- bourhood. On the arrival of a body of police, the pri- soners retreated into the house again, and commenced a fusilade of bricks and other missiles on the officers In the meantime a large crowd had assembled. and the greatest ex- citement prevailed. The police overpowered their assail- ants, and arrested theprisoners in the home, the injured persons being conveyed to the infirmary.—The prisoners were remanded for a week. The fourth annual amateur athletic festival pro- moted by the ironworkers of Warrington was held on Saturday, in the field adjoining St. James's Church, Latchford. The weather, unfortunately, was not all that could be desired, rain falling in the early part of the day, and also at intervals during the afternoon, and consequently the attendance of spectators was considerably less than would doubt- lesS have otherwise been the case. The com- mittee having again offered some handsome prizes, a goodly nnmber of entries for the various events were received, and, in the local events especially a large proportion of competitors turned out. The ground•was in a some- what sloppy condition owing to the rain, and this, while adding to the discomfort of the spectators, made heavy work especially for the bicycle riders. At the conclusion of the sports the Mayoress (Mrs Harrison) distributed the prizes to the winners. Alderman DAVIES, in moving a vote of thanks to the Mayoress, said the sports had been conducted in such a way as to do honour to those who had the management of them. (Hear, hear.) With regard to athletic sports, it might be known to those present that wherever a nation had prospered there had been sports of that kind. These sports in no way interfered with ccimmercial or literary pur- suits, but rather proted an advantage to them. (Hear, hear:)—The Rev. S. WILKINSON seconded the proposal, which was carried with acclamation.— The MAYOR, in acknowledging the compliment ori behalf of the Mayoress, said that sports of that kind need not interfere with other duties, and were cal- culated to make life pleasant and to stimulate pluck and determination which were valuable quali- ties. He preferred athletic sports of the character they had witnessed to football, as he had read so much about that game that he almost shrank from witnessing a match.—Mr. T. Mortms said that com- plaints had been made about the want of variety in the sports, but he hoped there would be a greater variety next year., and that they would go in for walking and jumping matches. (Hear, hear.) During the afternoon selections were played by the League hall Band. It may also be mentioned that the proceeds of the sports are to be given to the Warrington Infirmary.

A painful sequel to a suicide has occurred at Oldhatn. John Taylor, landlord of the Coach and Horses Inn, Reyton, hung himself, and Mr. Ralph Mello!, mernba- of the Royton Local Board, on seeing the body, was seized with paralysis and died shortly afterwards. SHOCKING SUFFERINGS IN AN OPEN BOAT.—The Royal mail steamer Kinsembo, from the West Coast of Africa, re- ports having rescued at sea, in an open boat, two men who had been eight days without food or water. The boat hid originally four occupants, but two of them died of their suf- ferings before the Kinsernbo fell in with the boat. When the Kinsembo was near Old Calabar, an object was descried in the distance. It appeared to be a canoe, but no occupants were visible, but, for fear there should be anybody in the tiny craft, Captain Liversidge ordered the signal whistle to be blown, ta draw their attention. In a moment or two there slowly rose from the bottom of the boat the form of a man. The steamer's course was then altered, and on coming up to the canoe it was found to contain two natives, one of the poor fellows lying helplessly at the bottom of the boat. The two men were then helpei on board, and the doctor of the steamer attended them. When they had sufficiently re- covered they told a pitiful tile of suffering and death. They were fugitives from Prince's Island, fleeing from the Yoke of their Portuguese masters. They had then been about eight days without food and water, except- ing some salt water, which only made their their thirst more intense.

div.head: NTTER. LONDON OUR
div.p: NTTER. LONDON OUR

LONDON, THURSDAY. The House of Commons resumed business yester- day after the shortest Whitsun holiday known tol history. It is sitting again to-day. But there ba little interest in the proceedings, and very few pre- sent to partake in them. Mr. Gladstone himself has cheerfully set forth on the war path, and already this evening the telegraph wires are bring- ing echoes of his triumphal progress north war'. His example has been followed by the great bulk of members. There remains only a melancholy resi- duum, largely composed of members who do not intend to offer themselves again. It is a depressing scene. sad not without due cause. Less than six months ago the House of Commons met full of life and vigour, overflowing the limits of the chamber, and clamouring for more room in which it might carry on the business with which it was charged. Nearly one half of the assembly was composed of new members, who thorOughly enjoyed their new position, and looked forward to long continuance of its enjoyment. Then Comes the blind Fury with abhorred shears, And slits the thin spun thread. It is pitiful to think of all the labours given in vain, all the money wasted, all the ambition brought to a sudden and final close. Not the least dismal reflection is found in the con- viction that those who, having fought the Generall Election in November and won, again in July will find themselves before their constituen- cies within six months. The era of comfortable long Parliaments is temporarily over. From 1868 to 1874, from 1874 to 1880, from 1880 till the win- ter of 1885, these were tenures ' for which it was worth fighting. But the game is not worth the candle when it comes to Pavliaments cut off before they are six months old. Yet the only certain thing about the Parliament which the people are already engaged in selecting is that it cannot live more than six months. Supposing Mr. Gladstone be returned with a working majority and carry. the Government of Ireland Bill through in Octo- ber it will be thrown out by the Lords in December, and there would be the necessity for another appeal to the country on a question perhaps involving more than Home Rule for Ireland. If on the other hand Lord Salisbury is brought into office and begins his twenty years of coercion there will be such an earthquake in Ireland, such chaos at Westminster, that the country will perforce be asked to interpose between the contending forces. We shall then have a strong ministry, whether un- der Mr. Gladstone or some other Liberal chief, at which the question of Home Rule for Ireland will be finally settled as it might have been in the cur- rent session but for the defection in the Liberal ranks. There never was an election pending the issue of which was more darkly clouded. The Conservatives are jubilant, and with good reeson. Having nothing to lose, any variation in the situation can only be in their favour. They see the Liberal house divided against itself, and confidently await its fall. There is little doubt that in many instances they will benefit by the split in the Liberal party which they have so sedulously nurtured. In places where they have no chance of running their own candidate they will use all their influence in favour of any Liberal candidate who has declared against Liberal policy in Ireland. Such members as Mr. Peter Rylands and Mr. E. A. Leatham feel themselves secure in the conservative vote, though with what kind of con- science they will subsequently take their seats in the House of Commons as Liberal members remains to be experienced. In the Newport division of Shropshire, in the Malden divi- sion of Essex, and in South St. Pancras, dissentient Liberals who had felt themselves secure in the promise of the Conservative vote have already been undeceived. In each of these cases Conserva- tive candidates will oppose them, and as the sece- ders cannot expect to receive the Liberal vote, Con- servative victories will be assured. In many boroughs Conservatives, having the Irish vote turned against them, will lose their seats, probably balancing these gains made out of Liberal dissen- sion. On the whole the fact remains that the most probable issue of the general election will be a searching change in the personnel, whilst the balance of parties will be pretty much the same. I hear from one of Mr. Gladstone's intimate as- sociates that both his health and spirits have risen in prospect of the fight. Even his voice feels the in.spiring influence of the situation, and has so greatly gained in strength that he faces without anxiety the prospect of the campaign. I hear a story, for the truth of which I vouch, which illus- trates the remarkable influence he wields over his colleagues. On Wednesday, in last week, when the Cabinet met after the vote on the second reeding of the Government of Ireland Bill,Mr. Childers was met in Pall Mall by one of his colleages in the Cabinet. "What is it to be ?" said the colleague, 'Resignation or Dissolution?" "Oh, resignation by all means," said Mr. Childers emphatically, "It would be the greatest folly to dissolve just now." This vie strongly held by the Home Secretary, was shared by Sir William Harcourt, and possibly by one or two other members of the Cabinet. It appeared certain that there would at least be an animated discussion on the subject. When the Cabinet met, Mr. Gladstone produced his familiar quarto sheet of paper covered with notes, and observing that the Cabinet would probably like to hear his views on the question at issue recited eleven reasons in fa- vour of dissolution. This was exactly an argument apiece for the members present, and it sufficed. Not a single voice was uplifted in objection to or even in discussion of the proposal, and after an un- usually brief sitting dissolution was unanimously agreed to. The General Election will probably hasten the -return to this country ef Mr. Samuel Plimsoll. He is at present, or was when I last heard of him, in the United States. Like some other members of the House of Commons, lie invested considerable sums of money in the purchase of land in Florida, antici- pating a peaceful and prosperous career as an • orange grower, "what time" the New Zealander is sitting amid the ruins of St. Paul's. Unless Mr. Plimsoll has greatly altered his mind, lie will pro- bably reappear on the political stage. Americans are, by the way, growing uneasy under the passion of recent growth with English capitalists to pur- chase land in the States. A bill is now before the Legislature making it illegal for aliens to acquire land in the States. It is a somewhat arbitrary measure, of the kind peculiar to Republics. Of course, it cannot be retrospective, and will therefore be inoperative over enormous tracts of land already purchased by Englishmen. I know one quiet look- ing member of Parliament who owns a large slice ' of the suburbs of the city of Denver, a crime of which no one to look at him would suspect him. There is, I fear, no chance of the recovery of Mr. Escott. His name still appears upon the cover of the" Fortnightly Review." But he is practically ' disabled for work. A movement, strongly backed, is now on foot to obtain for him a grant from the small fund at the disposal of the Prime Minister for the relief of those who have fallen in the struggle for place in literature, science, or art. No reply has yet been received, but it is probable that if there is any money available Mr. Gladstone will listen to the plea. It is supported by persons so widely separ- ated in political life as Mr. Chamberlain and Lord. Randolph Churchill. Both these gentlemen are per- sonally acquainted with Mr. Escott, and their sympathy for him in his trouble led some- time ago to a curious little sensation in the political world. It happened on the night when a report was circulated in a crowded House that Mr. Chamberlain had resigned. Immediately afterwards Lord Randolph sought Mr. Chamberlain in the subterraneous room which he had occupied as President of the Board of Trade and retained as President of the Local Government Board. The two were closeted together for more than half an hour, and rumours of a friendly alliance devised against Mr. Gladstone filled the House. They were, how- ever, only discussing the news of poor Escott's breakdown which had just reached them, and were devising means for his relief. So persistent was the rumour attaching to this meeting political sig- nificance that Mr. Chamberlain found it neces- sary to send a conisaaniqueto the papers denying the report. Mr. Browning is at work IPT on a new poem. Ha says he has three parts of it complete, but hesitates to name an appropriate date for its publication* grinds Like the mills of God, Mr. Browning slowly Half a dozen lines completed in a day is a triumpl; of progress. Moreover he has other calls upon his time than those of the Muses. He is, I should -the most indefatigable man-about-town that Lon- don knows. One sees him everywhere—at lun- cheon, dinners, suppers, probably balls, certainly five-o'clock-teas, where he stands cup and saucec hand the benevolent centre of a group of adoring dames. Ladies do not read Mr. Browmng's poetry. In fact it is only people of resolute mind and stan- ding shoulder to shoulder in regularly formed " So- 'Cieties " who do; but they like his talk and love to bask in his benign fatherly preSence. The season has been killed by the crisis, and al- ready it is spoken of in the past tense. In music it

has been the most prosperous and the most event- ful season we have had for years. We have had Liszt and Rubenstein and Moszkowski. The latter has had quite an ovation, and I think one of the rea- sons is that he is a Russian. Wagner has been over- done, and Rubinstein has brought Russia into fashion. It seems incredible that a three-syllabled musician, the first two syllables of whose name gave the word Moscow, and the third the word Ski, could be anything but a Russian. As a matter of fact he is a German, born at Breslau two and thirty years ago, and a pupil of the Berlin Conservatories, where he studied under Kullak. His success has been a surprise to himself and an astonishment to Rubin- stein, who has netted over .£5,000 as the rusult of his experience of the depressed state of trade in London.

div.head: Xatterti to titt editor.
div.p: Xatterti to titt editor.
PRIMROSE DAMES AT WORK.

Sir,—The modest and bashful primrose is going out of bloom; its beauty is fading. But not so with the Dames of the League; they are just at this time displaying ,an unusual amount of life. Several ladies of the Primrose League are putting themselves to the trouble and danger of hearing things they won't like by making in this neighbourhood a personal tour of the farmers' and working- men's houses, and distributing tracts on the Land Ques- tion, showing the unreasonableness of the labourer in seek- ' ing to possess "three acres and a cow." Of course, the Tories think a good cottage garden should satisfy his ambition. Will some working-man ask the Primrose Dames the next time they come around to let him have the cow and three acres on trial, and to return both in case they should prove so troublesome to him as the Tories pretend to fear they will ? I, for one, intend to ask them if they breach the question to remain, yours respectfully, PLEBEILCN. Frodsbam, Jane 15th, 1886.
