div.head: BAD TRADE AND THE TORIES.
div.p: BAD TRADE AND THE TORIES.

Sir,—lf the present stagnant state of trade does not waken workmen up to a sense of their duty, I scarcely know what will. Those who simply look on the surface of things are apt to say, "It matters little which of the two parties holds the helm; they are both alike, each looking out for themselves." There may be some truth in this, but if it continues a truth the working-man will have himself to blame. The question, who shall be our member? is one quite within the power of the working-man to settle; and the sooner he cries out, "A plague on both your houses," and determines to send men of his own class the sooner will he be on the way to alter things. Taxation is a wide subject', and quite beyond my rower to deal with in an ordinary letter, yet in taxation lies the problem now waiting to be solved. We maintain immense armies, yet in time of need are without an army. We ply away immense sums of money to a pauper class, yet never have an officer to lead the soldiers in battle. Our navy and its deficiencies forms a stock subject in the House, and n.Yer fails to win support when mere money is wanted. We spend immense sums on 40-ton guns, and then resolve that they are useless. We sell war ships by auction, and then buy them back at a much increased price. Omittine• Sundays our "preparations for war" cost us close upon-- £94,000 per day. Think of it! Agricultural landlordism costs us £200,000 per day, a'cherished institution this of the patriotic Tory. Two dukes have a united in- come derived from rents and royalties of £3.680 per day. To the members of the House of Lords for supposed ser- vices we pay £730,654 per annum, and if your readers will excuse me I may just whisper that we have paid to the Queen for kindly condescending to open Tory Parliaments since her ace-scion 43.210,000. Perhaps it will be right to say that the Queen's immediate relatives have joined at this small item.

Another item I should like to know something of is, what sums are paid in ground rents to absentee landlords? Work- ing-men must understand that the rents for all our mills, factories, shops, and cottages are paid to men who, in scarcely a single case, reside amongst us, and therefore con- tribute nothing to our rates.

All the instances given above mean taxation, mean so much dead weight on labour, mean reduction in wastes, and will continue to grow worse if Toryism is upheld. By sup- porting Liberalism we gradually, if slowly, pave the way to a better state of things. Labour has to-day 12 represen- tativee in the House, brewing 24, manufacturers 69, law 110. If working-men think that the interests of the brewer, the lawyer, and the manufacturer are of more importance than the removal of taxation, why let them still be sent to Parliament, and the sooner we shall become what the Tory employer wishes us to become. In one of your contemporaries recently appeared a letter, written by a Tory manufacturer. It deplored the present state of trade, and proceeded to give the cure, which was " merely to reduce our workmen to the same level as those of other countries." To accomplish this object it is only "necessary for all the capitalists of England to unite"; when this is done "some legally constituted tribunal—the quarter sessions or some such meeting of intelligent gentle- men " might then proceed to fix the wages. The writer thinks the "present absurd system of holding conferences" where the workmen and the employer meet and agree what wages shall be paid, is simply "killing the goose that lays the golden egg." Why, this Tory employer asks, should commerce be " fettered " by employers being called to pay such "exorbitant wages when in Germany the workman is satisfied with 2e. 2d." for fifteen hours? True to the Tory instinct, he longs for the "last century when wages were fixed annually by county justices, and rarely exceeded 61. per week." Think of this, Tory working-men, you who are striving after a share of the good things of life, and who dare to place yourselves a little higher than the squire's hunter, or the dog in his kennel. It has been thought that the English working classes

div.head: TRE FXAMINER, SATURDAT, JUNE 19, 1886_
div.p: TRE FXAMINER, SATURDAT, JUNE 19, 1886_

could be successfully compared with any other class in the 1 world; but this is also a mistake. Our Tory friend goes on to say—" Were it not for the superior cast of countenance; it would be difficult to distinguish the young ladies and gentlemen of the superior orders from the sons and daugh- ters of the common worker, so far have they carried their extravagance in dress." This reminds me of the notice sent by the Tory landlord to the village schoolmaster. "All the villagers desirous of coming to my house approach it in a becoming and respectful manner, i.e., through the back way and to the kitchen door. There is not a farmer in the place who ever has had, or would have, the impertinence to do otherwise. I desire that in future you will do the like. Lyonel Tollemache." How loving these Tories are. Be- lieving that all men are equal in the sight of God, they do their best to make them understand the wide difference there is on earth between ' ladies and gentlemen" and the "sons and daughters" of the mere "common worker," even , to insisting on approaching their august presence by tha "back way." With the Tory employers' 6s a week we should very likely be told to adopt the Duke of Norfolk's advice, who, in pro- posing the toast of "The industrious lalourers" at a din- ner at Steyning. said, referring to curry powder, as a food for the poor, "If any gentleman will try and take a pinch and put it into hot water, I don't mean to say it will make good soup; but this I say, that if a man comes home and has nothing better it will make him warm and go to bed comfortable. (Laughter.) I mean to try it among my labourers, and by doing that I.am sure that if the winter comes on severe we may add very much to the comfort of the poor. (Suppressed laughter.") The "Times," in a leader on this, mentioned that "pepper water was used on the Conyngharn estates in Ireland for the purpose of render- ing the pangs of hunger less intolerable." Our Tory employer no doubt sees his way clear when he advises that employers should pay their workmen such wages as they "find convenient," or in case of their refusal that they should "be treated as vagabonds." A corres- pondent of the "Times" writes that "at Seraig the aver- age wage earned in the mines is about 2s 3d per day. With such wretched wages there is small need to wonder that the men are discontented. On Sundays they may get a little meat or sausage—the latter made of pork or horse flesh. Four horses are slaughtered weekly for this purpose, the animals are descritad as being old decrepid, tough, but not diseased, theit flesh being wholesome but nasty. The men's families never have even butterine to their bread, and, under such circumstances, all other articles that make life endur- able are dispensed with; consequently all the small local tradesmen are on the verge of bankruptcy." It is for a state of things like this that the columns of a British paper have been used for purposes of praise. Well may this Tory employer say—" The Education Act was a mistake, the Household Suffrage Bill a crime." Without these his dream might have become a reality; with them, it will be the peoples' own fault if we make one more step towards such a wretched condition of things.
CLIFFORD DIX.

ACCIDENT TO A LOCAL ATIILETE.—The greatest sym- pathy is expressed in athletic circles at the sad accident which befel J. U. Newsome, a promising bicyclist, and the winner of the championship cup offered by the Cyclist whilst running at Liverpool, on Saturday. Newsome was scratch man, and whilst attempting to pass other com- petitors, he was knocked down and had his lea broken very bAdly. He is now an inmate of the Royal Infirmary, Liver- pool.

HITYTON PARK BAND or HOPE.—Considerable disap- pointment was felt by the members of the above branch of the St. Helens Band of Hope Union at the miserable state of the weather which prevented their annual out-door demonstration on Whit-Monday, according to arrangements made similar to last year. However, the best under the circumstances was done. The children and adalt members of the association mustered at the Park Schools at one o'clock, with the Whiston brass band, under their leader, Mr. J. Corns. The capacity of the schools was tested to accommodate the numbers, and tea was served whilst the band enlivened the proceedings. After tea, the weather having cleared a little, a procession was form, headed by the handsome banner, a large number of flags also being car- ried by the juveniles, who marched through Huytoa and Huyton Quarry.

SERIOUS ASSAULT ON THE POLlCE.—Thomas Raby, a rough-looking young fellow, living in Mount-street, Ec- cleston, was charged with being drunk and disorrlerly in Liverpool-street on Saturday night, also with assaulting P.C.'s Edward Caunce and James Wild, and further with damaging Caunce's uniform to the amount of 2s.—Superin- tendant Johnson stated that constable Wild was unable to appear, and he must ask for the prisoner to be remanded.— P.C. Caunce said he had seen P.C. Wild that morning He was not able to walk, and could not get a boot on his feet. About a quarter past eight on Saturday night the prisoner was drunk and fighting in Liverpool-street. He refused to co away when requested and used abusive language. He was taken into custody, whereupon be threw himself to the ground and commenced struggling and kicking violently. On the way to the station be struck and kicked both officers several times, and in the struggle be tore his (wit- ness's) coat.—The prisoner was remanded until Friday.
WALKING DAY AT WARRINGTON.

The Walking Day festival which is so anxiously looked forward to by Sunday school scholars, but which is in Warrington also regarded as a general holidew by adults, was celebrated yesterday. The weather has recently been a very inconstant quan- tity, sunshine and rain having alternately prevailed, there being, however, a considerable balance in favour of the latter, so that early yesterday morn- ing the signs which are commonly held to predict the meteorological character of the day were eagerly scanned. These signs, however, were not of a very decided nature, The clerk of the weather was, if we may speak somewhat lightly of that mysterious personage, "sitting on the fence" as it were; and,it was hard to *ay on which side he would come down. There was consequently some apprehen- sion that the day's enjoyment might be to a great ex- tent marred by climatic influences, but fortunately anticipations of this kind were not fulfilled; for, though the day was a dull one throughout, the rain kept off, and the pre-arranged programmes of the different schools were carried out. The streets were aiive at an unusually early hour with neatly- dressed children who were making their way to the respective schools, and at some points banners and festoons were hung out from places of business , and private residences. Most of the shops remained closed, and some few were only opened for an hour or two in the morning. Large numbers of people were also to be seen making their way to the station, evidently intending to spend the day out of town, and as a result the eailway officials were kept more than usually busy. Liverpool seemed to be the destination of the bulk of those who left town, the International Exhibition at, that place no doubt being a great centre of attraction. Soon after nine o'clock processions of school children began to make an appearance in the various streets, the long strings of scholars, the varying uniforms and re- sounding music of the bands, and the floating of the innumerable banners combining to make a very ' animated and pleasing scene. Spectators turned out to witness the spectacle in great numbers, so that at Market-gate and some other points the streets were almost impassible. With prudent forethought the Mayor had issued a notice prohibiting vehicular traffic in Bridge-street, Sankey-street, Bewsey-street, Bold-street, Horsemarket-street, Buttermarket- street, and Irlam-street, between the hours of nine o'clock and half-past twelve, and this had the effect of making locomotion much easier and safer than it would otherwise have been. Large however, as was the number of spectators, it was noticeable that the crush in such central places as Sankey-street was not so great as on some former occasions. As usual, the Church schools defiled into the Park, and were formqd in lines in front of the Town Hall, and subsequently proceeded by way of Parker-street, Wilson-Patten-street, &c.,ito Mar- ket Gate, at which point the larger part turned down Buttermarket-street on their way to the Parish Church; others, such as St. James's and Holy Trinity, going to their own places of worship, at each of which there was a short and suitable ser- vice. Several of the schools in connection with other places of worship had independent proces- sions pre,-ious to setting out for the places at which they were to spend the remainder of the day. One of the most noticeable of these processions was that of the Catholic s?,hools of St. Alban's and St. Mary's, which was a very long one; and another very inter- esting feature was the procession of the Salvation- ists, who, following out the commendable plan they have adopted on other occasions, had drawn to- gether the very poorest children of the town. The appearance of many of these children, not a few of whom were hatless and shoeless, betokened the hardness of their lot, and many a commendation was passed upon the "Army" for having thus thrown as it were a gleam of pleasure on the lives of the neglected waifs of the town. It is needless to say that throughout the procession there was a profuse display of banners, large and small. Some of the larger banners were very handsome and beautifully designed. The smaller ones, as a rule, cantained scriptural and other suitable texts or mottoes. In the matter of banners the Catholic and Salvationist processions were, probably, the most noticeable. The Catholics, as usual, carried off the palm for richness,variety, and beauty of display, many of even their smallest banners being extremely handsome. The Salvationist' flags, on the other hand, were noticeable on account of their simplicity, and some, of them bore signs of having seen much service and gone through many a "fray." In the afternoon the streets of the town were ex- ceedingly quiet, and at times seemed almost de- serted, but as the evening wore on the returning scholars and excursionists again (rave life to the scene, and it was not till a late gave that they assumed their normal appearance. THE LATE KING OF BAVARIA. THE FUNERAL.

The late King Ludwig II will be laid beside big uncle, Prince Adalbert, in St.. Michael's Church at Munich. It has been provided that the cortege shall not pass through those streets which, by means of as idiosyncrasy King Lud- wig was wont to avoid in his lifetime, especially the Maxi- milian-square and Maximilian-street. It is thought that the cortNe will take four boars to reach the church. The body will be entombed in a vault, three seals will be affixed, and three keys to the coffin will be distributed, one apiece to the Grand Master, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, and the churchwarden. Immediately after the body shall have been placed in the tomb the King's heart, under an es- cort of cavalry, will be conveyed to the Pilgrimage Church of Alt o)tting, where the hearts of all the dead Bavarian Princes are inurned.

LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The House met at 4 o'clock. Several bills were forwarded a stage. On considering the Electric Lighting Bill as amended, Viscount BURY protested against a new clause giving further powers to local author- itiee.—Lord CAMPERDOWN supported the clause, which was finally rejected by 37 to 24.—Lord BROUGHTON intimated that on the motion for the third reading ;he should move its rejection. The lnternatioaal Copyright Bill passed through committee.—Earl SPENCER moved the second reading of the Medical Amendment Bill, which was agreed to.—Lord KIM- I3ERLEY. in answer to the Duke of Richmond, read a telegram similar to that read by Mr. Bryce in the Commons rela- tive to the New Hebrides. The House adjourned at a quarter to six. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The House met at 4 o'cloc' . ENGLAND AND THE UNITED STATFS.—Mr. BRVCE, re- plying to Mr. Baden Powell, said the Unitrl States-Govern- ment desired to deal with the facilities for commercial in. tercourse between the British lediee and the United States as a whole, and they were not yet in a position to state the course that would be proposed. He had no objection to produce the correspondence if required. THE NEW HEBRIDES.-1115 BRYCE, replying to Sir H. Holland, said the House won be glad to hear a telegram from Lord Lyons that day. It stated that Lord Lyons bad seen M. Freycinet who informed him that no information bad been received from New Hebrides on the point of hoisting the French flag, but the French Government bad telegraphed to the Governors of New Caledonia instructing them that if the hoisting of the French flag had taken place it should at once be discon- tinued. No intelligence confirming the reports in the news- papers had been received by the French Government. SICK SOLDIERS AT ASSOTIAN.—Mr. CAMPBELL-BANNER. IttAN, replying to Mr.: Morton, .?Aid that undoubtedly great mortality existed among the troops at Assouan. Sir F. Stephenson would remove as many sickly troops as possible to Cyprus. The force to remain at Assouan was in the discretion of Sir F. Stephenson. There was no desire on the part of the Land Commissioners to press harshly on the glebe our6basers. The Appropriation bill passed through 'Committee and was ordered to be read a third time on Monday. BENTINCH moved its rejection. He condemned the measure as thoroughly unworkable.—Sir J. Lunnocir defended the bill,. and contended it would do good.—Mr. C. Timis opposed the bill.—The third reading was carried by 84 to 17.—Sit H. thousand. They had three bands, one of which had came from Stockport. In the afternoon the children were massr4 on the green in front of the Town Hall, and the Salvationists neglected no device to secure to the waifs and strays tempo- rarily gathered under their wing a few hours of down-right enjoyment. Oranges and fruit were distributed at intervals, and a more substantial meal, in which ham sandwiches played a prominent part, was served out. The supply was not stinted, but no difficulty was met with in disposing of the eatables. It is worth mention that the Mayoress (Mrs. Harrison) was present with the Army at their dinner-time, and busied herself in helping to look after the wants of the youngsters. In the evening a public tea for the " soldiers " and friends was provided in Academy-street barracks, and a meeting was held later on.

ST. 'MARY'S CATEOLI—C.—The scholars of this school, to the number of about 500, gathered at the schoolroom, Bat- termarket-street, at nine o'clock, and, accompanied by about 120 members of the Children of Mary class, proceeded through the various streets of the town. They were headed by the League of the Cross Brass and Drum and Fife Bands, and were under the charge of the Revs. Fathers Sumner, Morgan, Fishwick, Duggan, and Mr. John Mullin, superin- tendent. Shortly before 12 o'clock they returned to the schoolroom, where the scholars were dismissed till two o'clock in the afternoon, when they again assembled and proceeded to the field near the Dog and Partridge, Manches- ter-road. Here tea and suitable refreshments were served out and games engaged in till evening. ST. ALBANS' CATHOLIC.—The programme of this school was similar to that of St. Mary's. About 800 scholars gathered at the school in the morning, and, under the leadership of the Rev. Fathers Murphy, Brown, and Hur- -1 worth, joined in procession with St. Mary's scholars. In the afternoon they also went to the field off Manchester-road, and there spent the afternoon. BLun COAT.—Number of 'scholars on books, 26 boys and 21 girls; average attendance, 26 boys and 21 girls ; namber of teachers, 2 male ; number of books in library about 400 ; governor, Mr. E. Rose. These scholars were headed by the band of the school.

PADGATS INDUSTRIAL.—Number of scholars on books, 105 boys and 80 girls; number of teachers, 2 males and 2 females; number of books in library, 72; superintendents, Mr. and Mrs. Mines: chaplain, Rev. S. Wilkinson. After taking part in the procession, headed by the band of the school, the scholars were taken to a field kindly placed at their disposal by Mr. J. Houghton:At Padgate. WonKtrousE.—Number of scholars on books, 60; average attendance, 54; number of teachers, 1 female; superinten- dents, Mr. and Mrs. Mackey; chaplain, Rev. S. Wilkinson. The scholars Nned the procassion in the morning, and went to the Parish Church ; in the afternoon they were served with tea and buns in the Workhouse grounds, and amused themselves with various games.

NE.gfj TON-LE-WILLOWS.—A home-and-home match having been arranged between the oho-to clubs, the first part of the game took place on Saturday afternoon_ oil the Bank Quay green. The weather alternated with sunshine and rain, notwithstanding whiell there was a fair number of spectators, and the green was in good condition, The visitrtrs arrived shortly', before two o'clock, and after they had about an hour's practice the game was proceeded wit"- The competitors, 16 aside, were first drawn , couples and afterwards singly. The result PTO' Warrington to be victorious in both rounds by 14 points, principally owing to Mr. Roughley and hi: ' partner scoring 13 to their opponents 1 in the gre round, and Mr. Joseph °leave 11 to nil in the second round. Most of the other games were of .6 close character, and great interest was centred I 1 them. The teams afterwards sat down to a knife fork tea provided by Mr, Mellor. After tea, tn." Newton president, in reply to the toast of the health of the visitors, congratulated both teams o_lll the harmonious manner in which the games been carried out. The rest of the evening wa' spent in an enjoyable manner. ALLEGED SHOCKING ASSAULT.—At the Wariine ton Borough Court, on Wednesday Patrick nart' labourer, 11, Silver-square, a young man, ly*e brought up in custody under the Criminal Law. Amendment Act. He was charged with criminallY assaulting three little girls, each 11 years of ages and named Martha Ellen Wilcock, daughter of Jane Wilcock, 24, Pinner's-brow; Mary Balmer, daughter. of John Balmer, 46, Pinner's-brow; and Elizabeth Lawton, daughter of Elizabeth Lawton, 43, Pill: ner's-brow. Mr. J. L. Whittle, deputy town 001'1 appeared to prosecute, and said that he only pro- posed to offer sufficient evidence to justify a remand of the prisoner, against whom there were, he men - timed, five distinct cases with respect to the threl girls named. On the afternoon of Sunday,. the 237 May, the three girls, after being at Sunday went for a walk. When in Orford Avenue the)" met prisoner, who got into conversation with thou; He got one of them across his knees, andpullea another against his chest. They ran away. r,rii soner follow ed and caught Balmer and another go• and committed the offence with which he Wtie charged. The other acts with which he was charr- were committed on another date. The Bench re- - schoox manded prisoner until next Monday. He was re- moved, strongly protesting his innocence. WHIT-MONDAY AT WARRINGTON.—TWO CirClll3l' stances tended to distract from the holiday charac- ter of Whit-Monday in Warrington this year. oil ' of these was the very unfavourable weather, an_.", the other the other the occurrence of the popillr, holiday of Walking Day in the same week, whlc.l: made many people who could indulge in only el"' "day off" select the latter. The morning of Mere day opened in dullness, there being evident of rain, which were confirmed later on by an alines'. continual, though not violent, downpour. As a eett" sequence considerably fewer excursionists left the;, town than is customary on Whit-Monday. By the: Cheshire Lines, we understand, there booked f' Manchester about 120, Belle Vne 60, Southport 70; and 300 to Liverpool, -weich at present contains the- unusualattraction of an exhibition. By the Londe' and North-Western Railway about 150 went to Si: Helens, 120 to Widnes and Runcorn, 150 to Fre"' sham, 60 to Blackpool, and 50 to Chester. In the, town itself there was nothing of an unustu nature, though most of the places of business we closed in the latter part of the day at all. even- In the evening music was discoursed in the park 14, St. Paul's Sunday School Band, under the leadershiP of Mr. R. Smith, and; the weather having becoln. more favourable, the-selections were enjoyed by,s fair attendance of listeners.

TO THE ELECTORS OF THE BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON. GENTLIMRY, Having been unanimously chosen by the Council of the Liberal Association to contest the borough at the coming elec- tion, I have with pleasure consented to be the Liberal candi- date. I have lived amongst you all my life, and for the past live and thirty years have taken a warm interest in promoting the principles of the Liberal party. My political opinions are well known. I am in favour of perfect religious freedom and equality. I am in favour of and will support the voluntary and de- nominational school system. I love peace and condemn war I am in favour of the enforcement of the strictest and sound- est economy in all branches of the public serviee. I will, to the utmost Of ray ability, assist in the reduction of the bu,den of taxation caused by our enormous national ex- penditure, which at present falls far too heavily upon the shoulders of the working clams. All measures calculated to foster and improve the Trade d Commerce of our Great Empire shall have my most cor- dial support. The one great and important political questicn now before the Country is Mr. Gladstone's measure of Home Rule for Ile- land, and you will have to decide at the Polling Booths whether on are in favour of giving to the Irish Nation a Domestic Legislature under conditions such as to maintain the honour and consolidate the unity k• f the Emplre, oi whether you will support Lord Salisbury's policy of Twenty Years more of Coercion, and the banishment from the land of their birth of another million of Irishmen at a ccst of Fifty Million Pounds Sterling. If you elect me as your Representative, as I hope and believe yon will, I shall earnestly support Mr. Gladstone's measure for the Government of Ireland, because, in my opinion. it will spread Peace, Contentment, and Prosperity throughout the Sister Isle, and will bind Great Britain and Ireland in an Union stronger and more real than has ever ex- isted before. I remain, Gentleman. Your old and faithful Friend, JOHN CROSFIELD. Walton Lea, Cheshire, June 15th, 1888.
